Mr. Speaker, yesterday on the orders of the day the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) asked a question concerning communication between Japanese repatriates now at Vancouver awaiting transportation to Japan and local persons. It was anticipated that these repatriates, who are groups from Ontario, Manitoba and Alberta, would go on board ship within a day or two after reaching Vancouver. However, there has been a few days' delay in the arrival of the second ship in Vancouver, owing to the necessity for completing ship repairs, and it has been necessary to provide for the housing of these people in the immigration sheds at Vancouver in the meantime.
There are a number of people in Vancouver who want to talk to these repatriates, and it has been found desirable to make orderly arrangements to limit communication of this nature to responsible parties who have legitimate reasons. We have appointed an officer for this purpose, and all reasonable requests are being met. It must be remembered that the supreme allied commander in Japan has prescribed strict limitations on the types of currency, securities for money, and nature of personal property which can be taken on board ship, and the government is responsible to see that these provisions are complied with. Priority in time of staff and repatriates at Vancouver is being given to the carrying out of these provisions. I may say that the first ship is in dock in Vancouver to-day, and repatriates are being placed on board.

subtopic: CURTAILMENT OF PRODUCTION IN STEEL PLANTS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply based on a telegram which I have received from the steelworkers union in Sydney, a copy of which I have sent to him. Was it on the fuel controller's orders that operations at the Sydney plant in the production of steel have been drastically curtailed? If so, can the minister give the house any valid reason why conditions in a section of the country which is badly affected by unemployment should be further aggravated by this order?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Reconstruction and Supply):
speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CURTAILMENT OF PRODUCTION IN STEEL PLANTS
speechtext: As a result of an order of the fuel controller, coal suitable for conversion into coke has been moved to St. Lawrence ports to relieve a very serious lack of domestic fuel. This situation has resulted from the coal strike in the United States. Every hon. member will appreciate that if any considerable body of labour goes on strike, other bodies of labour are affected. That is the situation in this case. It has been necessary to take coke from another steel plant in order to relieve an urgent demand for domestic fuel. I hope the situation is reasonably temporary, but as long as the emergency lasts it will be necessary to continue this diversion.

subtopic: CURTAILMENT OF PRODUCTION IN STEEL PLANTS
speechtext: Has there been a curtailment of steel production in other plants across the country?

speakerposition: Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CURTAILMENT OF PRODUCTION IN STEEL PLANTS
speechtext: Yes, particularly at Sault Ste. Marie. Coke taken from that plant is resulting in a limited curtailment of steel production. The curtailment is entirely in connection with the production of steel rails, which happens to be a form of steel which is not urgently required. I understand that the production of steel rails has been curtailed at Sydney and Sault Ste. Marie to provide coke for domestic purposes.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
In view of the fact that these estimates will not be before the house for another year, I was hoping that the minister would have been able to hold out more hope to the committee as to the intention of his department to cooperate with provinces which are prepared to discuss with the federal government plans for the future. It was demonstrated during the war that the health of the Canadian people was a matter of national concern. In order to wage war effectively it

was found important to recruit healthy men and women and provide them with the very best medical, dental and hospital facilities. Many of these young men and women, for the first time in their lives, were able to have the most up-to-date treatment in times of illness. Many of them have now been discharged from the armed forces and are returning to various parts of Canada which have not the facilities which they enjoyed while in the service. Young men and women from my area, for example, left a district in which we now have three dentists to serve 57,000 people, or one dentist for 19,000 people. In the service, whether in the army, navy or air force, there *was one dentist to every 500. It is going to be very difficult to explain to those discharged from the forces how Canada during the war from 1939 to 1945 was able to supply one dentist for 500 people when both before 1939 and after 1946 these young people will have to live in communities so sadly lacking in these facilities.
The situation is nearly the same so far as medical personnel are concerned. In my area we have ten medical doctors serving a population of 57,000, which works out at one doctor for 5,700 people. In the very excellent report which has been presented, prepared by the Canadian medical procurement and assignment board, is given an analysis of the supply of doctors and dentists across Canada. It shows a very wide variation. In Prince Edward Island there is a doctor for 1,659 people, and the figures for the other provinces are: Nova Scotia, 1,450; New Brunswick, 2,136; Quebec, 1,206; Ontario, 1,068; Manitoba, 1,438; Saskatchewan, 2,078; Alberta, 1,626; British Columbia, 1,168.
It seems strange that in Saskatchewan we have the lowest ratio of doctors per thousand of people of any province in Canada; yet we recruited more doctors .per thousand than any other province. I am happy to say that many doctors from other provinces are now turning longing eyes to Saskatchewan with a view to practising there. It would be very difficult for Saskatchewan to provide out of her own resources the medical, hospital and dental services -which the service personnel received during the war, and so I think this is a matter of national concern. In Ontario you have paved roads and good telephone communication all over the province, so that a doctor can answer a call at a few moments' notice, and in that province there is one doctor to 1,068 people. But in Saskatchewan we have very few miles of paved road, a very small mileage of gravel road, and huge distances to cover, and we have only one doctor for 2,078 people. Up in the northern area where I live we have

Supply-Health and Welfare
only one doctor for 5,700 people. It must be recognized therefore that this is a national problem and that the people living in these remote areas should have made available to them the type of services that Canada can provide.
The table regarding the number of dentists is similar. In Prince Edward Island there is one dentist to 4,272 people, and the figures for the other provinces are:	Nova Scotia,
4,345; New Brunswick, 6,442; Quebec, 4,134; Ontario, 2,587; Manitoba, 3,881; Saskatchewan, 6.095; Alberta, 4,945; British Columbia, 2,743. This works out at an average of one dentist for 3,477 people. In the armed forces there was one dentist for every 500 people. Young men and young women in the prime of life in the armed forces would normally require a minimum of work done on their teeth, and yet they had one dentist for 500 people, whereas the average for Canada is one dentist for 3,477. Obviously there is something wrong. The federal department of health should at this stage be prepared to indicate the pattern that might be followed, and also make it clear that the department is prepared to go along with any province that will proceed to introduce a programme to meet our needs. I realize that it would be impossible in any part of Canada to have the ideal set>-up next year or the year after, because it takes many years to train doctors and dentists. But we should be proceeding in the field of health in exactly the same way in which we proceeded in the field of defence during the war. Disease is an enemy that we should be worrying about. I will mention two of our most serious problems.
In the publication entitled "Health, Welfare and Labour"* a reference book prepared for the dominion-provincial conference,, on pages 14 and 15 we have statistics in connection with the death rate from tuberculosis. Only two provinces in Canada are giving complete and free treatment for tuberculosis, namely Saskatchewan and Alberta.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Alberta comes first.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
No, Alberta does not have to come first. Alberta did not introduce free treatment as soon as it was introduced in Saskatchewan. I cannot take credit for the free treatment in Saskatchewan for the C.C.F. government, because the service has been provided for many years. We in that province found twenty-five years ago that it was good business to spend money on preventing the spread of tuberculosis and providing free treatment for all those who suffer from it, and for many years we have had one of the lowest death rates in the world. If you leave
the Indian population out of the picture, in 1943 Alberta had a slightly better record than Saskatchewan; the death rate in Alberta was 18-2 as compared with 18-3 in Saskatchewan. But consider Manitoba, right next door to us, where you have a similar group of people under similar climatic conditions, but where they have not been as progressive in dealing with this problem: there, the average between 1938 and 1942 was 48-2 as compared with 28-7 in Saskatchewan. If you consider the death rate among Indians you have the shocking figure of 1421 in Manitoba. I am not proud of our figure for Saskatchewan, namely 752. It is away out of line with what it should be in a modern civilized society.
During the war I visited the United States hospital at Churchill, Manitoba, and talked with some of the doctors there who had made emergency flights to visit some of the Indian communities. They said, "You Canadians should be ashamed of yourselves for tolerating the conditions which prevail in many of these Indian communities where the original settlers in Canada have been denied medical, hospital and dental services." They said, "We understand you spend large sums of money in sending medical missionaries to China, India and Africa. That is a fine gesture, but why have you not been concerned about providing hospital, medical and dental services for your own Indian population?" I find from the analysis made by the department that in the past the provinces have not been able to deal with the problem adequately, and it is not too much to expect that grants should be made available to provinces which carry out a scheme which complies with the minimum set by the federal authority. More beds are needed in most of the provinces; and I think, until the federal authority takes a greater interest in this disease, we are not going to be able to show for all Canada statistical results such as we have in Saskatchewan.
I should like also to refer to the pages of this publication which deal with the analyses in connection with, mental diseases. Practically every province in Canada is very short of facilities for mental patients. I find that in most provinces there is an excess of the daily average population over the bed capacity in mental hospitals, as shown on page 23 of the report, running to as high as 61 per cent in British Columbia, Again our statistics for Saskatchewan are not satisfactory; we have a very large number of patients there in proportion to the number of beds available, but plans are now being made to correct that condition. In Saskatchewan we are trying to face up to these problems.
Supply-Health and W-elfare

The premier of the province is the minister of public health; and on the resources which we have available they are trying to establish new patterns. I was interested in seeing in the last number of Health an article entitled "Winged Samaritans", by Christian Smith, telling of the air ambulance service provided by the Saskatchewan department of health. In the article it says:
It is believed to be the first government-operated service of its kind on this continent. Courageous bush pilots have dashed into the subArctic on mercy missions.
So far as the writer knows, it is the first time that any government or department of health have provided this service. Last night I had guests in for dinner-a young chap back from the navy, and his wife, who is a trained nurse. She was telling me that her brother, a former R.C.A.F. officer, owes his life to the service of this Saskatchewan air- ambulance. The taxpayers of Canada, according to a figure quoted by the former minister of national defence for air, spent approximately $28,000 on training him to be a navigator. He had served his country faithfully, and after discharge became critically ill at his home at Wadena, Saskatchewan, last winter, and there was no hope for his recovery unless he could get away to the city. He was unable to make the trip by train, but in a few hours the air ambulance was sent down, the trip was made safely, and while he has not yet completely recovered it is felt that he owes his life to this service. I do not know how many lives have been saved by this air ambulance service; but there is no reason why the people of this country, who made that kind of provision for casualties during the war, should not be prepared to provide it for citizens in peace time.
I remember being at the Dafoe airport during the war. I was going through one of the finest small hospitals one could expect to find, where the patients were receiving the very best of care. One of the patients was not .-esponding as rapidly as might be expected, and while I was there the air ambulance came in from Winnipeg. Nobody asked how much it cost to bring that ambulance from the city; the only questions asked were, "Is there an air ambulance available?" and, "Is there something which can be done in Winnipeg which cannot be done in Dafoe?" The answers were, yes, and this young airman's life was saved through his being transported to a city which, by air, is really quite close. I think the federal department of national health should be prepared to give some assistance to all isolated localities in Canada where the local authorities would be prepared to cooperate in providing air ambulances for sick people.
	-
I think the federal authority might also be expected to make grants to try out some experimental work in new fields. Last winter I visited in Oakland, California, the Kaiser hospital, an institution which has done such a spectacular job during the war. There were about 80,000 workers in the shipyards for whom complete medical and hospital services were available at the hospital. Doctor Garfield, who is in charge of the hospital, in one of the articles he prepared for the medical association explained that this was not a very popular project with the members of the medical profession; they frowned on any form of group practice where doctors worked on a salary. The scheme embodied three major principles: free treatment, group practice, and adequate facilities. It is true that the doctors who were working on salary were not receiving as much as many of them would have received in private practice during the war, but they were getting salaries of from $5,000 to $15,000 a year, and they were working approximately an eight-hour day. Of course a doctor, if he was in the middle of an operation, did not put away his instruments when the eight hours had passed, but on the whole they worked around a 48-hour week. They had some time for golf and fishing, and they worked as members of a team. They had adequate facilities.. They built hospital accommodation to care completely for the eighty thousand who were working there, and the patients, the members of the staff and the people in the community were loud in their praise of this type of project. I cannot see any reason why the federal department of health should not be prepared to make substantial grants to the provinces that are ready to do experimental work in fields such as I have suggested. I suggest that before these estimates are brought down for another year, the minister endeavour to work out some technique whereby the provinces that are prepared to take seriously the analyses and recommendations made by the federal government during the last four or five years in the general field of health may be given some assistance so that we shall have experimental work carried on in the several provinces.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I am very much interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Mackenzie, particularly as they concern the question of tuberculosis. I congratulate the province of Saskatchewan on the work they have done in regard to tuberculosis. Their programme is at least twenty-five years old; but the hon. gentleman stated that the only free treatment given was in Alberta and Saskatchewan.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Complete.

Supply-Health and Welfare

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I should like to point out to him that Ontario has been for some time holding chest clinics in towns throughout the province. A chest clinic with complete X-ray equipment comes to my own town twice a year. Appointments are made through doctors, and everyone caring to go, or cases referred by doctors to the clinics, will have diagnosis made, and in the event of their being tubercular' they are taken care of in the sanatoria of the province. At the present time also, in Ontario, mass surveys are being carried out. People in the towns in my constituency are being X-rayed. Next week 4,300 will be X-rayed in my own town, without cost to them. There is a shortage of beds, but that is being taken care of.
The hon. member also pointed out some of the benefits derived from practising medicine in Saskatchewan. I would never have believed that such a condition existed. I cannot believe that doctors are getting $15,000 a year and working forty-eight hours a week.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That is in California.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman suggest it is so in Saskatchewan?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Not yet.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Does he hope it will be? I should like to ask the hon. gentleman what would happen in case his wife were ill.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: They have a large staff of fifty or sixty doctors working as a group in the X-ray clinic in Oakland. The doctors do not lay down their instruments in the middle of an operation. If a doctor works sixteen hours one day he does not come to work the next day. They organize their work in such ' a way that the doctors put in approximately forty-eight hours a week.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: That would be impossible in a rural district where one doctor has charge of the district.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: This is in Oakland.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Often a doctor in a large area will work twenty hours a day as an hon. member suggests.
There is one question I should like to discuss this afternoon. In going over the estimates I find little in the way of grants for public health research. This is something that has been neglected in Canada. Little research has been carried out by the dominion, and very little by the provinces. The high incidence and high mortality in certain diseases would indicate that they constitute problems which should be subjected to intensive research. If Canada has reached the status of a nation, the responsibilities of a nation in the protection of the health of its
citizens should be undertaken by the state. That applies to research, which I am especially considering this afternoon.
In the closing days of the previous session, during the discussion of the health estimates, I inquired of the Minister of National Health and Welfare as to the research being carried out in Canada at the present time.. He replied that it was being carried on by universities, hospitals, institutes, "and the like", with assistance from the national research council. This is far from an ideal situation, as it is only by advancing our knowledge that effective or preventive treatment can be accomplished.
Let us consider the disease of cancer. Cancer kills one in every eight people in Canada. In view of this serious situation, Ontario is at present carrying on a campaign for subscriptions to the Ontario cancer fund, to be used for the purpose of dealing with this dread disease. In Canada the King George V silver jubilee cancer fund, raised in 1935, amounted to $500,000. From 1937 to 1940,_ $14,000 was paid out of that fund each year to the cancer committee of the Canadian Medical Association. In 1940 it was agreed that half of the grant should be paid to the association. In 1942 the grant to the association was reduced to $7,000. I would like to point out that this is a cancer fund raised by the citizens, and not money voted by the government for cancer research or treatment. It was, however, pointed out by the minister that cancer research is being carried on in England and the United States, and that if we were to do anything effective "we would have to do it on a large scale as we do not wish to duplicate the work being done in other countries." It would seem from this reply that our attitude in Canada is to wait and follow the results of research in other countries. This suggests the question, do we wait, in Canada, until a cure has been discovered? It would seem to be the attitude of the department, in spite of the fact that this disease is responsible for the death of one in every eight people in Canada. Everyone is acquainted with the long course of the disease and the terrible suffering it causes.
I have had pathetic requests from all over Canada for research in respect to arthritis. Almost every member has had such requests, though possibly I got more than my share. It is a disease of long duration; it has been called Canada's No.. 1 crippler-. The cause is not known. No accurate records are available, but the number of sufferers from this disease is estimated at from 100,000 to 400,000, and it accounts for a greater number of days lost than from any other chronic ailment except nervous and mental diseases. Sir Kingsley Wood, British Minister of Health, says, "Rheumatism

Supply-Health and Welfare
among insured males is responsible for 16 per cent of the total sickness and disablement." In Canada there is only one hospital equipped for specialized treatment of arthritis, and they accept only seventy-five paying patients. Millions of dollars are spent annually by patients for treatment, but it continues to cripple and deform, and those afflicted suffer untold agonies. Apart from the loss to the industrial life of the nation, the outlook for those afflicted is dark, suffering as they do from a disease without any known cause or effective treatment. Under present conditions there is as yet no ray of hope to brighten their lives. No work is being done by the national research council regarding this disease.
The seventh cause of death for all ages in Canada is tuberculosis. It is the first cause of death for the age group 15 to 45. Thirty thousand Canadians died of tuberculosis in the years 1939 to 1943. Saskatchewan has carried out a campaign to control this disease within the province for many years. Ontario has a very active campaign at the present time, and mass X-rays of the population are being conducted. Not only is there a very high mortality rate, but owing to the fact that it is so easily transmitted from an infected to a healthy person, every means should be taken to arrest the disease. The high death rate in Canada calls for investigation and research.
Last fall I asked the minister certain questions regarding maternal and infant mortality. There is no research being carried on; it is largely confined to educational programmes. The high infant mortality rates in Canada are much higher per one thousand live births than in England, United States, Australia or New Zealand. In a young and growing nation such as ours we cannot afford to lose such a high percentage of our future citizens. As regards maternal mortality, our rates are comparable to Australia, slightly below the United States, but not as good as New Zealand, England and Wales. These facts would indicate that we are remiss in our duty if further investigation is not made into the cause of these high mortality rates.
According to the statement made by the minister last December, research in Canada is carried on in institutions such as the Banting institute, Toronto; the Connaught laboratories, Toronto; McGill university, and other hospitals and laboratories. He also stated at the last session that research at present is not a function of the federal government, and not very much function of the provincial governments. It may therefore be called nobody's child at the present time.
Let us take, for example, one institution, which I had occasion to visit a week or so ago. I became interested in the marvellous 
work being carried on in this hospital, the neurological institute of Montreal. Patients are admitted for neurosurgery from all over Canada, and in fact all over the world. They had patients from Palestine, from Arabia, from every country of the world. The outstanding results in neurosurgery obtained during the last war are largely the result of the research, carried on by Doctors Cone and Penfield; and not only does this institution do its own work, but it trains young surgeons in neurosurgery. After three of four years' training these young surgeons go out all over Canada, in fact all over the world, to carry on this work. It is one of the finest institutions of its kind; yet it has been starved financially. It would be a dire calamity if this institution were forced to close its doors and the research should have to be discontinued for lack of funds. It has done much for the cause of humanity.
It is true that the demand for research will entail the expenditure of money. But we might very well curtail expenditures in other matters, as there is no problem we face which is more important than the health of . the people.
One Sunday in February I listened with much pleasure to a radio address of the minister, in the course of which the minister said-this is as close as I could get to it:
One measure of a nation's greatness is the efficiency with which it cuts disease and death rates. We have been satisfied too long with the provision of hospitals for the care of those who should not be ill and the provision of charities for those who should not be poor.
I fully agree with the minister's statement, but I should like to point out to him that in Canada we are doing very little to elimin- . ate the diseases responsible for the highest percentages in our death rates. The suffering of those afflicted by a disease such as cancer should in itself be sufficient to stimulate more concentrated research for knowledge of causes and cures.
The standard of our Canadian universities rates very high among educational institutions in the world. Our medical colleges and the science faculties of our universities are graduating many students who are anxious to carry on research and are capable of doing it. It is an unfortunate fact that on graduation many of them are forced to leave this country and become citizens of the United States where there is a broader field and more lucrative positions are available so far as scientific investigation is concerned.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
When the committee rose last night we were discussing the formation of a standing committee on public health


Supply-Health and Welfare
and welfare. If I remember rightly, the hon. member for Eglinton included the subject of social security.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: And housing.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Public health and welfare and social security are matters which surely deserve the attention of any Canadian citizen. Certainly they are of sufficient importance to engage the attention of a standing committee of this house. There is in this country an aroused social consciousness in regard to public health, as evidenced by the success of and the interest taken in campaigns against venereal disease and cancer.
In the province from which I come, Saskatchewan, as my colleague the hon. member for Mackenzie has pointed out, much attention is being paid to these things at the present time. The government of that province has been criticized for the heavy expenditures on matters of health; but so far as I am concerned I am proud that four times as much has been allotted in the current budget for expenditures of the department of health as was allotted by any former administration. The opportunity, and I may say the need, for welfare work has been enormously increased in Canada by the recent war. I myself have been for some years connected with family welfare work, and I am amazed at the number of problems which arise in connection with returned service personnel. Wars always increase there maladjustments and produce the emotional upheavals which cause social disease. While I am on the subject may I point out that there is a great dearth of trained family welfare and social workers, and agencies have been compelled to carry on understaffed and without benefit of persons properly trained.
Social security has a distinct bearing upon public health and welfare. There is a lot of truth in the statement that social security would spell the doom of a great many of our social diseases. It is my opinion that the time which hon. members of this house might devote to the study of this subject in committee would be time well spent.
I should like to draw the attention of this committee to two or three things which I think should be studied by such a committee. I believe these matters have already been drawn to the attention of the government by the Canadian Welfare council. On their behalf, as well as on my own, I should like to put some of them on record.
First, a national council in the welfare field might well be set up to compare with the present Dominion council of health. Such a council might synchronize and correlate the work of the various provinces. Of this there
is much need. A national point of view would increase the general standard, and progressive action in one province, of which we have some examples already, would stimulate the action of other provinces along social service lines.
The second point is the confusion of residence-and I am thinking in regard to family welfare work in particular-in respect of eligibility for municipal assistance. When a person moves from one municipality to another he loses his right to assistance. He is nobody's child and so becomes a problem. I have in mind a case which was drawn to my attention last winter. A woman and her three children were living in a shack, and the only thing they had on which to live was the children's allowance which they were receiving from the government. The reason was that her husband, who previously had been a very good farmer, refused to cooperate in any war work; therefore he had been spending a period of three years in gaol or in work camps. This woman, unable to cope with the problems which she had on the farm-unable, for instance, to pull water out of a deep well for the cattle-moved into the city of Saskatoon. When her resources were depleted she became dependent upon the allowances of her children. It is an actual fact that nobody had any responsibility for her. The city, of course, had no responsibility, because she had not been long enough in residence. The province said they could not do anything for her unless she were to move back to the municipality whence she had come, and the municipality whence she had come said exactly the same thing. But the woman had not a dollar; she could not move anywhere, and if she did go back there she would have nowhere to live and nothing to eat.
In the same connection I might mention the case of a person taking temporary employment somewhere else, in a different town or province. What we appear to need is a channel cutting through which will enable people to move to different parts of the country in pursuit of their livelihood without jeopardizing their right to the social assistance they would have received in their former place of residence if such had become necessary.
Another matter is the consideration of methods of preventing people from escaping responsibility to their dependents by moving from their accustomed domicile.	It is a
problem with which we have had to deal in connection with some returned men. I was glad to see that the government of Saskatchewan passed a bill enforcing in Saskatchewan
Supply-Health and Welfare

maintenance orders made in England, Northern Ireland and all His Majesty's dominions. There was need for such legislation.
Another matter with which I think the committee might well deal is the giving of encouragement to young people who wish to join the. nursing profession or to take up family welfare work. I think perhaps the government missed certain opportunities when they released so many girls from the armed services following the end of the war, girls who would have made excellent material for such work because they had undertaken certain basic training.
So, sir, for the reasons I have stated, I wish to go on record as being heartily in support of the formation of a special committee of this house to study the subject.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Supply-Health and Welfare

partment of health is the most talkative health department I know of in the world, through radio, films and advertisements. What are we going to do about it?
Another matter relates to the schools for our rising generations. I remember when we had to carry on a long fight supported by the Toronto Telegram, to have medical inspection in the public and separate schools of our city, and the health department had to provide nurses to visit the homes and the people. This was a most commendable work, but the whole cost was placed on the taxpayers. I believe the department has done some good work but I submit the time has come when there should be more actual direct aid by bonus or subsidy in this connection.
The government is spending billions of dollars to-day, but in the days of Sir Charles Tupper, in 1896, the Conservative government was able to run the country on $36,000,000. Our population has not gone up more than a couple of million since that time. Before the war we got on with about $400 million for civil government, but now the cost of government has gone up by geometrical and arithmetical progression. There are many things we are going to need. If we are going to have a health department, let us have a health department, not some kind of a skeleton health department where they just make speeches and travel all over the civilized world. Let us have an up-to-date health department that will provide hospitals and other relief for our sick, for our mothers and infants, for the whole of our population. Let us have a real national health scheme, not a skeleton scheme that gets nowhere and does nothing.
Take cancer and many other diseases which affect the human race. What is being done in Ottawa about them? They are doing a lot of talking but when you get down to brass tacks you find that the universities and hospitals have had to do most of the work. Public health is too big a quetsion to be mixed up in politics. If this department is kept in politics there will be very little done.
I hope something will be done to provide more hospital accommodation and to help the municipalities in the work they are doing and relieve the heavy burden upon the taxpayers.
I have been speaking only of our own health department, but I think I can speak for the health departments in the surrounding municipalities. They are similarly situated and are doing grand work. The health officers of our cities work very hard for very small remuneration. I do think that at a time when we are spending so much in making hand-outs for breakwaters and all that kind of thing we should have a little pin money to hand back to 
the taxpayers who are paying the cost of all this. Something should be done to provide more nurses in Canada by releasing them from the services, which would not suffer any now. What are we doing with 20,000 of the forces in Germany? The United States is going to quit; and when the appropriate vote comes up I can give eight or ten reasons why we should reduce it and let a lot of these nurses come home.
I am very much surprised that we are voting $11,000,000 for national health and welfare in addition to the $285,000,000 baby bonus authorized by statute. I am not objecting to this if the money is properly distributed, but I know some well-to-do people who are getting the children's allowance, yet the old age pensioner gets pin money only and has to pass a means test.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to take a few minutes of the time of the committee to say a few things about -health policy in general, and more particularly to make a plea on behalf of the more than 400,000 Canadians who are afflicted with the crippling disease of arthritis. Some weeks ago I placed on the order paper a resolution which I hoped would be discussed, and I had hoped too that there would be a full-dress debate on this whole question of arthritis, because I feel that now is the time to begin to focus the attention of the public on this terrible disease and the widespread suffering it has been causing for some years.
During the past twenty years public attention has been centred on ways and means of combating such terrible killer diseases as tuberculosis and cancer. Public health bodies, medical men and governments over the Dominion of Canada have publicized their efforts and have combined their efforts so well that at the end of twenty years we now see that most excellent results have been attained through their efforts. To-day if tuberculosis and cancer are taken in time a cure can be found for them. This has been the result of the intensive efforts that have been made to deal with these diseases, and also the fact that public opinion has been aroused and demands that something be done.
But while our efforts have been directed towards combating the killer diseases, I am afraid we have neglected diseases such as acute rheumatism, and especially arthritis, which have afflicted and crippled about 600,000 people altogether in Canada. The hon. member for Lanark spoke about arthritis, and I appreciate what he said, but I should like to repeat this much. So far we have found no means of treatment; we have not even deter-

Supply-Health and Welfare
mined as yet the cause of arthritis. That ought to be enough, it seems to me, to spur us on to intensified effort. I am sure that much can be done in the next few years to alleviate the sufferings of arthritics if public health bodies and medical men will concentrate public attention on this disease. The only real attempt in Canada to give follow-up treatment and bring relief to arthritis sufferers has been made at Banff, Alberta, and even that has been entirely inadequate to meet the needs of the people.
As a matter of general policy it seems to me that the governments in Canada should concentrate first upon diseases which require long and costly treatment; those for which so far there has been found no cause, those which require intensive and careful investigation to find the cause, especially those which are proving such a scourge among the Canadian people. The reason I say that is this. Diseases like poliomyelitis, cancer, tuberculosis and arthritis can, because of their long and costly treatment, impoverish families. I have seen such impoverishment. We saw poliomyelitis, for example, strike in a family in Alberta during the height of the scourge that we had just a few years ago, and attack perhaps one or two of its members, and the family itself through the long and costly treatment required lost its entire property. This is a matter of grave concern, and it is time that the federal government stepped in and gave some assistance to prevent such impoverishment. That is why in Alberta we did start out several years ago by assisting in the treatment of tuberculosis, poliomyelitis-or infantile paralysis, as it is more commonly known-and cancer, through providing free government treatment and hospitalization as well as after-treatment and care for the sufferers from these diseases. We did this chiefly because we felt that no family should be allowed to be deprived of home and property and become impoverished by the long and costly treatment required to bring about a cure of these diseases. The result so far has been very good. Not only that; by focusing the attention of medical men and public health societies and organizations upon these diseases we have begun to find cures and the most effective treatments, which to-day are being extended free to the people of Alberta.
Now, it seems to me, is the time to extend our operations and to take in the field of arthritis. A substantial sum of money ought to be set aside by the government of Canada for that purpose, to be placed at the disposal of trained investigators, technicians and research workers who would combine their, 63260-130J
efforts with those of the research council in one all-out attempt to find the reason for arthritis which creeps upon and cripples people as it does, and to find a cure for it as quickly as possible. I do not mean the expenditure of just ten or fifteen thousand dollars. It seems to me that hundreds of thousands of dollars should be spent for this purpose, and this is the government that should do it. When the cure has been found, or the most successful treatment ascertained, the provincial governments through their own health departments can apply the cure or treatment successfully, and, I am sure, relieve the suffering of many hundreds of thousands in Canada. I would urge upon the government, and upon the minister particularly, that he see to it that a substantial amount of money be set aside this year, and that work be initiated at the earliest possible moment on this dread disease arthritis.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I rise principally to ask the minister, when he makes a statement on arthritis, to make it as complete as possible, and, if he will and if he can, to let us know something about the hospital to which the hon. member for Peace River referred, the one at Banff, which to my own knowledge has effected some amazing cures. To help him with his research I am going to give him an experience of my own; I have some excellent information for him. I have received 102-letters on this subject of arthritis; in fact there were so many coming in that I dictated a form, which I will read to the committee:.
I have your letter respecting arthritis.
For the additional reason that I am suffering from it myself, you may rest assured that I will do all I can.
At the same time I was receiving, as we all did, hundreds of postcards on the subject of everybody being retired, women at the age of fifty-five and men at the age of sixty, at $60 a month. Being my own secretary, and not being very efficient, I got some of my arthritis letters in envelopes addressed to people who -wanted $60 a month, and I will now read a reply I received yesterday, and in which the minister will find, I am sure, the cure for arthritis:
Dear sir:
After receiving your letter of 18th April, 1946, I have carefully scanned the card which I mailed (copy enclosed) to you, and to date I have been unable to find any reference to arthritis, so am wondering if you are trying to have some fun at the old lady's expense or if your stenographer mixed letters.
Since I have never had arthritis I cannot speak from experience but I have always heard , that if you were thoroughly stung by bees it

Supply-Health and Weljare

would cure the disease, so why not hunt a good apiary and stir up the tenants of two or three lively swarms of bees and of course you will then get stung and be able to speak from experience as to whether the rumoured cure is a success or not, and I wonder if you would be stung any worse at that, than the people of Canada have been in electing some of the present members of the house of parliament, of course present company is always excepted.
I am enclosing the second chapter of our serial which is being issued by card.
Now, haying become an authority, I should be glad to join in the research work. I will not undergo the test myself.
But, seriously, would the minister mind, when he does make his statement, if he and the department have knowledge of what is being accomplished at the seventy-five bed institution in Banff referred to a moment ago, where excellent work has been done in affording relief to friends of mine.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
When the estimates of this department were before us last session, the minister concerned, if my memory serves me correctly, received more bouquets and verbal compliments than all the rest of the ministers combined. I am -not at all afraid of these compliments having tgone to his head, but I do hope that they went to his heart, because if there is one [DOT]department of government more than any other which needs a heart it is the Department of National Health and Welfare.
[DOT] 1 have long believed that the health of the 'people should constitute a first charge on [DOT]nny government, and I should like to say =a word or two in support of what has been rsaid by the hon. members for Lanark and Teaoe Biver with regard to the need of those who suffer from arthritis.
I am sure that the prevalence of arthritis in Canada to-day has not been recognized either by the public or by the government as it should have been. It is a most serious disease, and one which makes an appalling drain on the efficiency and well-being of our people. There may be those who, reading these debates, will say that we have a medical profession and it is their business to look after this kind of thing. I am prepared to pay the highest form of tribute to the men and women of the medical profession, but I am sure that there is a task here which is beyond the abilities of our medical practitioners of to-day; I believe it is a problem which requires research and definite legislative action now. Up to the present time our health programme and proposals have been incomplete in not having recognized the need to deal with this disease which is so prevalent among our people.

A little while ago. the hon. member for Lanark said that we might have in Canada from 100,000 to 400,000 suffering from this disease. Those who have made a close and detailed study of it, people who are chiefly concerned about it, tell us that there are at least 690,000 cases of arthritis in Canada, all of them calling for relief. Here I would like to point out that there- are twice as many sufferers from arthritis as there are from heart disease, ten times as many as those who suffer from tuberculosis, and seven times as many as those who suffer from cancer. On Friday, September 14, 1945, the late Harry Leader, then member for Portage la Prairie, made an impassioned appeal in this house on behalf of those who suffer from the dread disease of cancer. I for one heartily concur in the appeal which he made; but, as I have already said, there are seven times as many arthritis patients as there are sufferers from cancer. Many of these, we hope, will be eventually cured, for it is admitted that early diagnosis and proper treatment will avoid crippling and in most cases effect a cure. Even where the case is well advanced and treatment obtained late in the progress of the disease great benefit is still possible. I have had personal experience of this. At the moment I am thinking of a lady in my constituency who spent several years in bed, a helpless cripple. We were able to get her to the Banff Hot Springs hospital under the care of a splendid physician, with the result that-after many months of careful theatment she returned to her home and her family, not cured one hundred per cent but certainly greatly benefited and able to walk. In other words, as a result of the rest and the treatment she receeived she is now enjoying a new lease on life. Before I left for Ottawa she begged me with tears in her eyes to make an appeal on behalf of those in Canada who suffer from arthritis as she has done.
I understand that in Sweden something worth while has been done along the lines for which I am appealing; for Sweden has no less than nine hospitals, each containing sixty beds-that is, 540 beds exclusively devoted to the treatment of arthritis. Naturally we are interested in what has been accomplished thereby. Reports reveal that sixty per cent of the patients three years after leaving the hospitals have returned to and are actively engaged in their former occupations, and the condition of another eighteen per cent is-so improved' that they need no further treatment.
Against this splendid showing of Sweden what is the picture in Canada? Here, as has already been stated, we hare one hospital con-

Supply-Health and Welfare
taining about seventy-five beds which are set apart for arthritics, but let it be clearly noted that these are for paying patients exclusively. Then where do the poor and the needy come in? Well, they don't come in at all; they just stay outside and continue to suffer until death brings relief to them. During the war years this country suffered great shortages of labour owing to war needs, and drastic legislation was introduced to remove various bottlenecks; yet all the time this particular disease and others continued to remove workers from their place in industry.
In order to strengthen my appeal I should like to read an item from the press relating to this matter. The following appeared in the Nanaimo Free Press of Friday, July 27, 1945:
A number of local people, many of whom have been victims of arthritis, are banding together in order that suitable representations may be made at the August 6 dominion-provincial conference at Ottawa regarding the growing need for combative measures in new legislation. They urge that this disease, termed "Canada's No. 1 crippler," should receive No. 1 priority rating on the conference agenda. The present means of battling arthritis are said to be wholly inadequate, with the result that its menace to public health increases at an alarming rate. It is a disease which causes great suffering, deformity and eventual incapacity, doing incalculable damage and causing immeasurable loss to the economic, social and domestic welfare of Canadians. Statements are to the effect that Canada now has 600,000 persons afflicted by this dread disease. Medical practitioners do an heroic best to offset its activity, but are handicapped by lack of suitable hospitals and equipment. Authorities now concur that in a majority of eases hospitalization is essential, including specialized treatments. Day to day observation and corrections are said to curb progress materially. Canada has but one hospital where such treatment is at present available. It is the mineral springs hospital at Banff and of this hospital Doctor Lowenstein of New York, arthritis specialist, recently said in an interview:
"The work that is being done in this hospital in combatting arthritis rates among the best on the continent and merits a new and better building with the very best of facilities. The combination of treatments used here is exceptional. and the results are excellent."
It is being urged that some provision be made in the national health bill for similar hospitals to be made available in every province.
We take pardonable pride in our national war effort. We recognized the tremendous forces that were arrayed against us, and we marshalled our forces against the threat to our way of life. We spared neither time nor effort nor money to achieve victory on land, on the sea and in the air, yes, and on the home front. We addressed ourselves to the task that was before us and, by the grace of God, we won. To-day I am asking that we recognize the fact that in Canada we have other enemies to fight and other victories to win. The battle against arthritis will challenge
our mettle, and here I would suggest some definite lines of action: First, that the national health bill should make provision for treatment of arthritis through special grants to the provinces for the erection of adequately equipped hospitals; second, that such hospitals be made available at Canada's famous mineral springs hospital, the mineral waters of which are invaluable in the treatment of arthritis ;[DOT] and third, that where suitable existing military hospitals are to be found, with their furnishings and equipment, those in each province should be allocated to the care of chronic rheumatism. I suggest this for the consideration of the minister, in the hope that something will be done for this very needy class of our citizens.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Those who have spoken previously have given a clear outline of the conditions that need rectifying. I recall that in the last parliament the then member for Swift Current, Mr. Graham, gave us an excellent account of the work which was done at Banff Springs hospital in connection with the cure for arthritis, and he spoke with reference to the treatment of members of his own family. At that time the minister stated that they were giving every consideration to this problem. I am sure that the members of this committee will be extremely disappointed if the minister gets up and makes what I was going to call the old routine statement that the department is giving the matter consideration, because that was over two years ago. Surely the department, having listened to the former member for Swift Current and to other members of this house relating certain experiences-we have had one to-day from the hon. member who has just taken his seat-will propose something concrete. It is not sufficient to say, after two years of warning from members on all sides of the house, that we are still 'investigating the subject. The country at large demands something more than that. The people demand action, because in the final analysis the disease takes a greater toll than the war itself and it is something that should be considered most carefully. I hope that in the time at his disposal the minister will make a definite statement to the house assuring us that the department is making progress, and will indicate the extent of that progress, so that the people throughout the country will receive some encouragement, especially those suffering from this terrible disease of arthritis.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I wish to make several observations with regard to one of the great scourges of mankind. It is tragic indeed that man will rally against the menace of war but will largely ignore his greatest, most elusive
Supply-Health and Welfare

and most unrelenting enemy, cancer. More than 65,000 Canadians died of cancer during the five years of the war. There were somewhat less than 40,000 fatal casualties as a direct result of enemy action. War is always a terrible tragedy when a nation loses its youth in conflict. I suggest however that Canadians are fighting a war every day against cancer; so far it has been a losing battle, and our casualties are increasing from year to year. But I believe that we can win that war if we go about it seriously in an all-out struggle to destroy this terrible menace.
Millions are spent in Canada on tobacco, liquor and the luxuries of life where only hundreds are spent to fight cancer, something much more deadly than the bullets of either the Hun or the Jap. There is still a long road to travel before our cancer research laboratories are adequately equipped to widen the field of human knowledge in regard to this dreadful disease. There is a lack of free cancer clinics, except in Saskatchewan, where one of two clinics handled five thousand cases for free diagnosis and treatment last year. Next to the diseases of the heart and arteries cancer kills more Canadians than any other malady. It is the No. 2 killer of men and women in Canada. According to the Canada Year Book 13,417 people died of this dread disease in 1941. By 1943 the number of deaths aad increased to 14,135 persons. Whether this increase is due to a more accurate diagnosis of the disease or not is difficult to ascertain; but the fact remains that more Canadians died of cancer in 1943 than in 1941. Authorities state that in six persons over the age of forty one dies of this disease.
An examination of the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare shows and appropriation for tuberculosis control but none for cancer control, despite the fact that there are less than one-half as many deaths form tuberculosis as from cancer. There should be a vigorous educational campaign to inform the general public about this disease. Knowledge is a powerful weapon in the fight to control any disease. It is a primary step. Generations of victims have either had the true nature of their illness concealed from them or have concealed it from their own families. Its appearance was thought to be a death warrant.
To-day enough is known by scientists about cancer to assure us that many lives can be saved by proper diagnosis and early treatment. It remains only for this information to be made available to the public so that the dangerous curtain of rumour, the halftruths and erroneous information can be torn aside.

Last month was set apart as a cancer month by the Canadian cancer society. This is a most commendable move. The purpose in doing this was to stimulate research, treatment and education in the field of cancer. The public appears woefully ignorant of certain facts about this disease. According to a poll conducted by the Canadian institute of public opinion more than one-half of our adult population believe cancer is incurable, or do not know whether it can be cured or not. Medical authorities have long insisted that the disease can be cured in the great majority of cases if treated in the early stages. About one-third of our population still believes cancer to be a contagious disease despite the fact that surgeons agree it is not. Most amazing of all, the survey conducted by this institute revealed that two-thirds of our adult population do not know any of the early symptoms of this disease. It seems to me that this is sufficient proof of the great need of a widespread educational programme.
I would suggest that as a supplement to the cancer month campaign just concluded, the Department of National Health and Welfare should conduct the most vigorous educational campaign to inform the public about cancer every day of the year by utilizing the facilities of the radio, the motion picture theatres, our schools and the press. This country must do all in its power to save from the clutches of this disease many people who through lack of kqowledge of its- early symptoms are doomed to a life of misery which all too often ends in horrible death.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Before proceeding with what I was about to say I think I should say a word, or two for the sake of the C.C.F. representatives from Saskatchewan. The hon. member who just took his seat recklessly remarked that there was a scarcity of cancer clinics in all the provinces but Saskatchewan. May I submit to him that he knows Saskatchewan, but he does not know the other provinces half so well; and if he will just talk for Saskatchewan and let those from the other provinces talk for their provinces I believe he will not misrepresent and mislead the people.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Are there any cancer clinics in Alberta?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: There are four, and they have had them for four years.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: How many did you treat last year?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Every person who has cancer in Alberta can come to a cancer clinic and get free treatment until he is cured or

Supply-Health and Welfare
until he dies. You cannot surpass that anywhere. I suggest to the hon. C.C.F. members that they are" so enthusiastic over their new' , government in Saskatchewan that they just do not try to give the rest of us credit for what we do. I just say that in a kindly way. Remember, there were social credit reformers in action in Canada several years before the C.C.F. got in action, and they were really doing things too.
I should like to say that the idea of having a health department in Canada is a good one. We feel glad that the health department has been organized. In our group we are satisfied that the total appropriation has been increased $63,221,407.73 since last year. This all indicates a sound attitude on the part of the dominion with respect to health and welfare in Canada. We recognize that under the British North America Act the responsibility for health services is primarily a provincial responsibility; but let it be borne in mind that this particular type of service is exceedingly costly, and that most of the provinces in Canada are very short of money and are limited in their resources with respect to getting revenue. It may be said that the dominion is likewise. That is not entirely so, because the whole power over financial policy in this country is centred in the Dominion of Canada, and is exercised by that dominion to the utter exclusion of all provinces. If any province undertakes to do anything in the way of progressive financial operations the dominion instantly rushes in and disallows its measures and declares them ultra vires, and all the rest of it. Therefore the dominion must take responsibility; if they will not let any province go ahead then the dominion has to go ahead. That is about all there is to say on that point.
In Alberta we have progressive ideas with respect to finance. We are positive they will work; the dominion is positive they will not work, but we notice that the dominion are very chary about giving them a chance to w'ork. So once more may I say that the dominion simply must find the money where the goods and services are available in the country.
I should like to urge upon the newly established Department of National Health and Welfare in Canada that it do not endeavour to duplicate the work which is being done by the provincial governments. There are two or three departments in Ottawa that seem to look over the whole field of activity, and endeavour to dabble in everything, that which the dominion ought to take care of and that which should be looked after by the provinces. The result is a duplication which
brings about waste and also destroys motivation, and has further undesirable consequences. The dominion should supplement the work of the provinces. I am not saying or implying for a moment that this is not the ideal of the present minister. The dominion should take the lead in coordinating the work of the provinces by calling regular conferences of provincial health ministers to decide upon desirable national objectives and the means of attaining them.
The main task of the federal department should be, first of all, to determine how to provide adequate grants in aid to the provinces to enable them to provide health services which they consider advisable. I think it will be found by each successive minister of health in Ottawa that the provinces will have progressive ideas of their own with respect to the kind of health services they desire. The records of Alberta and Saskatchewan already indicate the truth of what I am saying. The dominion does not need to undertake to tell any province what it is desirable to do. What the dominion needs to do is show the provinces how to do those things which they think desirable. Any deficiency on the part of the provinces does not arise from their inability to see what it is good to do, but from their financial inability to do the things they desire.
Another thing the dominion government must do is determine how to raise the Canadian standard of living. It may be argued by the minister that this certainly is not the business of public health departments in this country, but I am not so sure about that. What is the use of telling people the baby needs orange juice when in so large a percentage of cases throughout the dominion the parents are unable even to buy the baby the milk it needs, let alone orange juice. This would seem to indicate that the very first thing necessary is to set up or develop in Canada a system under which all those who are prepared to do their share of service in the dominion may obtain the means with which to discharge their responsibilities to their children as they come along, and to just as many of them as come along. I believe we can safely state that in this country one-third of the total population are in receipt of incomes so low as to render them unable to maintain a standard of living involving the bare necessities of life. In an age in which we have seen such a great development of scientific and mechanical skill; when we have such great power and other resources, that is a serious reflection upon the government which continues in operation in charge of the nation. Canada is
Supply-Health and Welfare

no exception. I believe the United States has a record far more blameworthy than that of Canada. But in dealing with this whole situation it is well to remember that there must be something radically wrong in the way the affairs of great nations like Canada and the United States are being managed to-day, or with the system under which they choose to operate, if we are unable to provide a full one-third of the people of our countries with the bare necessities of life. Until we learn how to remedy that problem, governments can expect a great deal of difficulty with regard to ill health.
If they propose to raise the standard of living, provision must be made for fair prices for goods, fair wages, and employment. Once more the minister may say that has nothing to do with his department. Well, if that has nothing to do with the minister's department, then the minister has not the power to deal with the health problem in Canada.
Very soon the question will be raised: where is the money coming from? I do not propose to go into any details with respect to that matter; probably I should be out of order if I did; but long before this debate is over we shall see the minister rise time and again and shall hear him remind us that he has not at his disposal limitless funds, and that he will be unable to do many of the things he would like to do because he simply cannot get the money. Before ever the minister says these things I am going to agree that it will be impossible to get from the people of Canada,, by taxation, enough money to do the things that need to be done in order to guarantee the Canadian people a proper standard of health. Yet the money must be found.
I agree entirely with the remarks of the other hon. members who have preceded me, that the first responsibility of a government in a country like Canada is the health and wellbeing of the people. The people are the greatest natural resource of any country. Let the people be weak; let them be unhappy; let them be unhealthy, and the efficiency of the country is immediately greatly impaired. Our problem ought not to be one of finance in this country; our problem ought to be one of goods and services. For example, if we want to know whether or not we can provide a dentist for every five hundred people in the country, let us say, as was suggested, the only question we need to ask is, are we raising enough young men and young women who are willing to go into our universities and acquire skill as dentists in order to provide a dentist for every five hundred people-if that should be the desirable number? The

answer would have to be, yes. unquestionably. It could not be answered otherwise, when we are afraid of unemployment and have experienced unemployment to such an extent as it has been experienced in Canada within the last fifteen years. If it is held desirable that there should be hospitals all over the country in order to care for people who are unfortunate, the only question we ought to ask ourselves is, can we get the lumber, the bricks and all the other things which are necessary to build enough hospitals? Can we manufacture the instruments required to perform the operations which will be necessary? Again the answer undoubtedly must be, yes, we can. Then these requisites which enter into the providing of a suitable standard of health for the country certainly are physically possible. If then, there is anything wrong, unquestionably it must be in the matter of finance.
Let the minister weigh that with great care. The other day, just as I was going out of the chamber he made a remark-of course not just because I was going out-about letting our money go to pot, or something of that sort. In making a remark of that kind the minister did not indicate the kind of vision a man of his age, in a responsible position such as he holds, should have, because he was entirely overlooking the physical possibilities of this country, its resources in manpower and materials. He was overlooking the fact that where the resources of a country in man-power and materials are such as to render it possible to provide a given standard of living in that country, then it ought to be able to have that standard of living; and if the financial system will not enable the countiy to have that standard of living something must be done with the financial system. Otherwise it , will automatically "go to pot." I do not wish to emphasize this over much, but we might as well have the cards laid on the table at the beginning of this debate, because before we are through there will be plenty of talk about money. Practically every person who rises in his place is going to demand or ask for some special kind of service which will cost money.
I suggest that the minister should not spend any of his time in the house bewailing the failure of the dominion-provincial conference. It seems there was a carefully laid out plan some months before the dominion-provincial conference took place to tell the country that if these provinces would only come together and humbly consent to allow the dominion government to have all the power it wanted, to take away from the provinces anything it wanted to take away, then thus and so would be possible; but if the said provinces should

Supply-Health and Welfare
not be cooperative in this respect, then all these fine dreams would be impossible of realization. I say, Mr. Chairman, that was not a very healthy thing to do. Since the dominion-provincial conference met we have noticed a tendency on the part of ministers to get up and whine about it, to say in effect, oh, we could have done this and this and this if the provinces had only consented to let us destroy the British North America Act, or take away their taxing powers, or do this, that and the other that the dominion wanted to do. I suggest that the minister do not do that; I suggest that he do not tell us that the dominion-provincial conference has to succeed in order that he may do the things that he needs to do.
The whole question is whether Canada can produce the goods and services necessary to attain the standard of living we desire. The standard of living we desire in this respect is a high standard of health and welfare. The only answer that can possibly be given is that we can provide the goods and services. Then then only conclusion that can follow is that we can provide the money and are going to provide the money whether the provinces consent to give up their taxing powers or not. That does not enter into the matter.
There is only so much money that can be taxed from the Canadian people. What the dominion gets from the people, the provinces cannot get. The provinces want, need and can use all the revenue that they can raise. It may be that there are certain companies so strong and so dominion-wide in their operations that no province can sufficiently tax them. If that is the difficulty, let the dominion come in behind the provincial taxing power with the power of the dominion. Then it will be found that the company concerned will see fit to obey the provinces. There should be no difficulty in that respect. All the money which the dominion could collect, if the dominion had the power to collect all the money, can certainly be collected by the provinces with the dominion's assistance. That is an aspect of the whole question which, for some strange reason, has never been emphasized in all the discussions entered into by dominion cabinet ministers, from the Prime Minister down.
I would advise the dominion cabinet ministers to forget their schemes for the centralization of power in Canada. Let them cease whining about the naughty provinces that have the wisdoni and courage to insist on maintaining their provincial power as given them by the British North America Act. let the minister lead out in exploring the possibilities of modifying our financial system.
Let him learn how to make our financial system reflect the facts of Canadian production and productive capacity. Let him learn how to make the Canadian financial system distribute the goods and services Canadians are able and willing to produce. Then the minister will find that he can obtain plenty of money to enable Canadians to have the healthful and abundant standard of living which is essential if we are to have a healthy and happy people. He will be able to find plenty of money to provide a system of health services federally supported but provincially and municipally administered, a system of health services that will cure all the curables and rescue all the unfortunate.
