Mr. Chairman, will' the
minister make a statement regarding rheumatic diseases which have been referred to by many hon. members? I have nothing further to add except to say that ways and means should be adopted across Canada to fight the inroads of these diseases. This matter was dealt with by the British Columbia legislature this spring when a recommendation was brought in by the select standing committee on social welfare and education, which read as follows:
Arthritis-Your committee recommends that, in view of the serious social and economic problems involved in the increasing incidence of arthritis and other rheumatoid diseases in Canada, the provincial government press the federal government for the establishment of the widest research facilities and the gathering together of all available information from all parts of the world as to the causes, treatment, and prevention of these diseases.
Further, that the provincial government on its own initiative should take steps to provide more facilities for diagnostic service, to increase facilities in existing hospitals for the more advanced methods of treatment for both indoor and outdoor patients, and the development of rest homes at suitable locations where all sound measures to help arthritis might be applied.
I have no doubt the minister has had this subject in mind for some time, but when he spoke earlier in the session I gathered that he was not convinced that it was necessary to do something at an early date. On page 420 of Hansard of April 1, 1946, hon. members will find reported an oral answer by the minister to some questions asked by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley). The minister pointed out that the associate committee on medical research of the national research council had been unable to do anything with regard to these rheumatic diseases during the war. He then went on to say:
The committee is. however, prepared to give consideration to applications for assistance in any project that gives promise of adding to knowledge regarding the cause methods of prevention



Supply*-Health and Welfare
or treatment of arthritis in the same way it does to other medical research projects. No such application is pending at the present time.
In the following .paragraph he dealt with the question of grants. Apparently a suggestion had been made that a grant be made to the Canadian rheumatic diseases association, but the minister said that he had been advised by the ministers of health of the different provinces that that association was not in a position to be given a grant at the present time. That may or may not be the case, but the answer the minister gave on April 1 caused me to have some doubt as to whether he realized how much people were concerned about this disease. I think it would be helpful if he would make a statement this afternoon.

speakeroldname: Hon. BROOKE CLAXTON (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is desirable that I say something at this stage on the various subjects which have been raised this afternoon. I am grateful to hon. members for their suggestions and comments and I want to tell them that I share many of the views that have been expressed. One general observation may be made with regard to much of what has been said this afternoon. Under any construction of the British North America Act, if the suggestions for action were carried out it would mean that the federal government would be taking action which ordinarily would be found to come within the constitutional jurisdiction of the provinces. At the same time that these suggestions are made we have other suggestions that there should be no duplication of the work done in the provinces. I find that almost every suggestion that has been made would have been met had the health proposals of the dominion and the agreement, of which they formed a part, been accepted and put into operation.
With regard to research, I would ask the committee to consider seriously whether they regard general medical and health research as an ordinary function of the federal government. At the present time we have two laboratories at Ottawa doing research work in connection with virus diseases, immunization and other health problems, including those relating to the Food and Drugs Act, and nutrition, but so far it has not been considered n proper function of the department to undertake fundamental medical research. One reason is that that kind of research is usually best carried on in connection with clinical opportunities which are to be found most frequently in la:ge centres where they have hospitals in

association with teaching institutions. That is not invariably the case, but it is so in many instances.
I would point out that the actual number of personnel qualified to do competent research work in Canada is definitely limited. I might call to the attention of the committee an observation made by Surgeon-General Thomas Parran of the United States public health service, when appearing before a committee of the house of representatives in the United States in connection with a bill to provide more money for cancer research. Surgeon-General Parran said that there are not as yet enough properly-trained cancer research workers even to begin the programme that was suggested. That is an important limiting factor on the volume and quality of research work that can be done in any locality at any time. It may be that in order to increase the total volume of research work in Canada we shall have to start further back and to provide fellowships to permit young doctors and technical experts to enter into research work and to train themselves by attendance at research and teaching institutions.
In this connection, too, I would point out that we have had the advantage of discussing the matter with representatives of the ministry of health of Great Britain, and the United States public health service as well as with officers of various foundations engaged in medical and health research. We have had several of those officers here at various times, and we have also entered into discussions with committees of the Canadian medical association and had interviews with many of the leading research workers in Canada, all in an effort to determine the proper field of research activity for the federal government.
Ever since the department was created on the 13th of October, 1944, barely eighteen months ago, this subject has been receiving continuous consideration and it still is receiving continuous consideration. But when you ask for action I must tell you that so far we have not been able to see any way in which action could be taken which would be likely' to produce favourable results and which lies within what has so far been regarded as the proper scope of activity of the Department of National Health and! Welfare. Since 1938 the national research council has had an associate committee on medical research and it has granted assistance to many people and to >
many institutions in connection with medical research.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Yes, I will try to do it. The national research council has been established by parliament as the principal agency of the federal government to carry on research. My predecessor and I have discussed with the council whether or not that function of the national research council should extend to medical research. We have decided that medical research should be assisted through the national research council rather than through the Department of National Health and Welfare. We came to that conclusion because we felt that it was desirable that practically all support of research by the federal government should be coordinated through one institution. The national research council has done magnificent work in assisting medical research relating to the prosecution of the war, but to a very great degree its assistance to medical research in connection with diseases not associated with the war had to be suspended because of the shortage of doctors and technicians in Canada. The pressure on the available personnel in connection with the war really exhausted all their possibilities of rendering useful service in any other field. But that has now changed, and with the demobilization of men from the armed forces, together with the continued output from the medical schools, it is expected that the medical research division of the national research council will be called on to assist in a very much larger number of research projects of various kinds.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Is there any liaison between the council and your department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I was just going to say that that does not mean that our department is not interested, because we are definitely interested and we are in continuous consultation with the research council just as it is in consultation with us. The deputy minister of national health and welfare is also a member of the associate medical committee of the research council.
I ask hon. members if that is not the sensible way to do it rather than to try to set up a duplicating institute of research for the federal government. In view of the resources available in Canada, it is our view that the best way to do this job is to assist in programmes of research being carried on in the places which can carry it on and are carrying it on and have the equipment and the trained research workers.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: You are entirely right.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: If we are wrong I certainly should like to know it, because then we might have to make some changes.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: The way is all right, provided that full use is made of it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
1 wish to say, too, that that is the way it is handled in the United Kingdom. The ministry of health there is a large ministry compared with anything we have in Canada because it renders direct service to the people; they have not a federal constitution. It has very great resources of personnel; it spends very large sums of money, and yet I understand that medical and public health research work is not carried out through the ministry of health but through the medical research council which does not come under the ministry of health but under three committees of the cabinet of which the minister of health is a member, but which report to the president of the council. I have had opportunities of discussing this with Sir Wilson Jameson, chief medical officer of the ministry of health, a distinguished public servant who came out on our invitation to discuss matters with us; also with Mr. Attlee and the president of the council. They have reached this conclusion based on their much longer experience in the field of public health than this department has had.
In the United States research work is carried on by the United States public health service in fields particularly related to public health. We do a certain amount of that work ourselves, either in our department or in other departments of the government. In addition, in the United States the public health service carries on cancer research through the national cancer institute which is located at Washington. I visited it and went all over the building with the director, and if hon. members of this committee could see the kind of equipment that is needed to organize research on cancer I think they would appreciate something of the nature and magnitude of the task before us. Cancer research is also carried on in the United States by a number
Supply-Health and Welfare

of teaching special institutions and institutes where large sums of money are spent, just as they are by the imperial research institute in the United Kingdom.
If I might develop the question with regard to cancer research for a moment or two, we know there is a very great deal of work being carried on in the field of cancer research. There is free interchange of experience and knowledge as they accumulate. If we were to start to establish an institute of the kind they have in Washington we would have to develop not only a great plant, which would duplicate the equipment there, but a trained staff which it would take years to gather. Then, if we accelerated our activities, we would be abreast of where the Americans are in this kind of project. That is not the only kind of cancer research.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Would it not be worth doing, though?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
We in Canada have great scientists, great doctors, great research workers whose names are known throughout the world. Canada holds second place to no other nation in these fields. Where we can proceed most intelligently is to see that anyone who is reasonably qualified to do research work gets the assistance necessary to enable him to do it, and, in addition, we could give some scholarships or see that scholarships were given in order to increase the number of research workers qualified to work in Canada.
This brings me to the King George silver jubilee cancer fund, to which the hon. member for Lanark referred in his interesting and helpful speech. To that fund, which was raised in 1935, a substantial contribution was made by the federal government. It was set up under a trust deed, and the trustees have full power to spend the money from the fund as they may wish. The hon. member for Lanark referred to what I said last night and gave from my speech last year the expenditures which have been made so far and which have been almost entirely on educational work carried on either by the cancer committee of the Canadian medical association or the Canadian cancer society. In no year has more than $14^000 been spent. The expenditure was made in that way on the advice of the cancer committee of the Canadian medical association, because the trustees could not see how during the war money could be intelligently spent on research in cancer in addition to the money which was available from other sources. But that situation is changing. The trustees have been meeting; we have examined the whole situation, and we have had a number of sessions with representatives of the Canadian
fMr. Claxton.l
cancer society and the cancer committee of the Canadian Medical Association, as well as the others I mentioned earlier. In consequence, not only are we going to give assistance again this year-one year more-to the Canadian cancer society in connection with its educational work, but we shall hold out the possibility of making grants to those who want to do research work in this field. In addition, we hope to establish a number of fellowships to train research workers.
While these developments have been going on, we have been having active discussions in an informal way with various provincial ministers and deputy ministers. There has been, the most general kind of cooperation; and I hope very shortly to call a meeting of those interested at which the fields of activity of the various organizations interested in cancer control work will be defined as well as they can be without putting them in straitjaekets. The objective will be a programme of work in cancer, using all means, which will mobilize all the resources that can be mobilized within Canada and to see to it that we do everything possible to find the cause and the cure of cancer.
There are four ways in which money can be spent in work in connection with cancer. The first is in the education of the public, to which the hon. member for Weyburn referred. That is necessary. It is necessary that it be brought home to people that if they have any of the symptoms-a lump or a tumour or a persistent sore throat or any of the other things-they should consult their doctor; and a large part of the money so far spent by the Canadian cancer society has been spent in just that work. We believe that organizations like the Canadian cancer society can carry on that work effectively. If there is a general desire that the federal government should go into the work of publicizing the need of early discovery and diagnosis and treatment of cancer, that certainly will be considered, because I believe we could do an effective job in that field, but it would remain -with the house to say whether that is a proper activity for the federal government to undertake.
The second way is the training of doctors to specialize in the diagnosis and treatment of cancer. As I believe hon. members know, there are only three established methods of treating cancer: radium, X-ray, and operation. As yet, there are no other established cures. These are effective only if used early enough. It seems to me that this work of enabling doctors to improve their own ability in this field can best be done by the establishment

Supply-Health and Welfare
of fellowships, by work through the Canadian cancer society, the Canadian medical association, through hospitals, teaching institutions, clinics, the provision of refresher courses, and the like. Certainly the federal government should not enter into that field at all.
The third way in which cancer work can be aided is by improving facilities for the treatment of cancer. That, it seems to me, is peculiarly a matter of provincial responsibility.
The fourth way is in research and the training of workers to do research. I have already mentioned this in relation to the subject of research, and I have nothing further to add to what I said in that connection. But I think I might say this. I am informed that it is a generally held opinion among those who are competent to say that it is unlikely that up to this day anyone who is really competent to do research in cancer has been held up for lack of funds. That is substantially true, though there may be exceptions.

As the hon member knows, a committee on Indian Affairs has been set up. I understand it is the intention of the committee to call officers of this department before it, and we shall make available all the information we have. When we come to surveys of some conditions among the Indians and Eskimos we still may have fairly sketchy material, but we shall make available all we have. While the results of our plans will not be spectacular at once, I hope that in a few years it will be possible to make substantial improvements in the health and welfare of our Indians and Eskimos.
Several hon. members have referred to the need for cooperation in this field. In my first speech in this connection I think I said, that cooperation was essential, as I have said the same thing to every other organization I have met in connection with the work of the department-. It has been my privilege to be invited to attend the annual meeting or other meetings of practically every organization working in' the field of health on a nation-wide basis across Canada. I have welcomed these opportunities and have gone to all these meetings with the hope of creating confidence and of establishing the foundation for real collaboration as well as cooperation. I believe that the general statements made by the officers of these associations have on every occasion, been supported by their members, and that their reciprocal promises of cooperation have shown by their works.
During the eighteen months that the department has been in existence, we have had, with very little exception, nothing but the heartiest and warmest cooperation from everyone working in the field. That applies to the
provincial officers, to the municipal officers and to the members of all professional and voluntary associations. This is one field in which there can be no room for competition. It has more than enough for everyone to do, and we have not failed to seek the assistance of everyone possible to make the best contribution we can to the work which we and they have in hand, namely, to see to it that as far as lies within our power we shall improve the health and welfare of the people of Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I listened with a great deal of interest to the minister, and I have no doubt that he meant everything he said, but after listening to him I am reasonably sure that he is not going to get very much activity in the field of medicine in this country until the government- are prepared to tackle two problems. First, they have to face up to the British North America Act and get away from this business of passing the buck to the provinces. That is one stumbling block which will offset about 75 per cent of what the minister had to say to us this afternoon. I do not wish to leave any doubt in his mind as to whether he is getting improvement or not when he makes the kind of statement and paints the kind of picture with regard to the future of health in Canada that he has done this afternoon.
Second, there is another problem that the government will have to face up to. They are going to have to tackle the drug manufacturers of the North American continent. There is a straight monopoly in drugs. The medical profession is largely hampered in putting on the market drugs that are already available in a form in which they could perform some service, because the drugs are pigeon-holed, curtailed, and kept off the market by the drug monopoly which exists on this continent. These are two things which will completely hamstring everything the minister had to say this afternoon.
I am not going to go into the matter of health in Canada. I think it is well known, and it- leaves much to be desired; but the federal government will have to face up to the two questions I have just mentioned.
With regard to this question of research the minister's statement also left me rather cold. He outlined so much machinery he is going to set up that his department will be completely fenced in, and he will not be able to break out of that ring. There is too much of it. It is like a committee. If you get twelve men on your committee, particularly if you include two lawyers, and want the committee to do a specific piece of work, the twelve men
Supply-Health and Welfare

start arguing and fighting and you get nothing done. If you boil it down to a couple of men, they will perhaps do something and ' bring in some sort of comprehensive report.
I am going to mention one specific matter on this question of research, following the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South. He asked the minister a specific question with regard to arthritis; what was being done and could be expected to be done. He gave the minister a golden opportunity to make a long speech, but he wound up without giving the committee very much information as to what would be done on the question of arthritis. The minister would lead me to believe, in his discourse to the committee, that he is pinning his hope on research to be conducted in Canada and the United States, and is not going beyond the borders of those two countries.
In June, 1944, as the Minister of Veterans Affairs will remember, I raised the question of arthritis in this house and pointed out that a drug known as ACS had been perfected in Russia which was guaranteed to cure arthritis and allied diseases. At that time I asked the minister if he would make some inquiries into the matter, pointing out that arthritis was responsible for the loss of more man-days in industry in this country than any other disease, and that, in addition, a large number of our ex-service personnel, particularly from the first war, were badly crippled, that our hospitals were filled with them. The Minister of Veterans Affairs, always cooperative, did what he could at the time by way of making inquiries and informed me that he could get very little information on the matter. Well,
I took time off to write the Soviet embassy in Ottawa, who referred me to the Mission of Alliance of Red Cross and Red Crescent societies of the U.S.S.R. in the U.S.A.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: I was referred there also.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
I wrote Professor V. Lebedenko, the representative in the United States of this organization, who replied on July 6, 1944, as follows:
A shipment of the anti-reticular cytotoxic serum is expected in the near future from Professor Bogomolets. Professor Bogomolets, however, in informing me of the shipment, asks that this shipment be restricted to laboratory and experimental use until such time as whatever research institute receives the serum is able to prepare a product identical with the original. Only after that time can it be prepared and released for general consumption.
It seems to me that the Canadian government or a responsible research institute should be able

to request a quantity of the serum from Professor Bogomolets through the Soviet legation for similar use in Canada.
Hoping that you will find this information useful . . .
Shortly after receiving that letter I saw in the Globe and Mail of July 10, 1944, an editorial commenting on this very question, from which I should like to read a short extract:
Gifts from Russia
While Britons and Canadians are sending relief supplies to the stricken people in Russia, the English-speaking nations are in turn receiving gifts from the Soviet Union. There has come from Russia, for example, the unique dandelion from which natural rubber can be produced and it is now being experimented with here and in the United States and England. Russia also sent recently a serum which may prove a potent w'eapon against rheumatism, arthritis, childbed fever, cancer, high blood pressure and perhaps also mental disease. This serum, known as ACS, is now being tested in a clinic by Lord Horder, chairman of the empire rheumatism council.
That is definite and specific information. I was surprised at the statement this afternoon by the minister of health. I did not expect the Minister of Veterans Affairs to get very much information on the subject back in 1944, because the drug was still in Russia and apparently the matter was in the embryo stage. But nearly two years have elapsed, and a Department of National Health and Welfare has been set up, with a minister and an adequate staff. The minister pointed out that it had a research department, and that research into various diseases was being carried on by the research council in cooperation with his department. If this drug known as ACS has the potential medical value indicated in the editorial I read; if it has been made available to the rheumatic council in Britain, through the chairman of that council, why has not something been done by the department and the research body in Canada to make that drug available to the people of this country?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: May I answer that question at once?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Certainly.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: More than a year ago we looked into that question, and I was advised there was nothing at all in it. I was advised of that by representatives of the Russian government as well as by the other people who had looked into it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
You were advised by representatives of the Russian government? I should be very much obliged if, before these estimates are passed, the minister would make available to this committee any correspond-

Supply-Health and Welfare
ence he may have had with representatives of the Russian government, stating that this drug had nothing in it at all. It was widely ballyhooed through Reader's Digest, through editorials and so forth, and the Canadian people were led to hope that they would receive some relief from this source. I received at least a hundred letters from people across this country inquiring as to the merits or demerits of this drug, and I should like to see some official statement by the Soviet people to the effect mentioned by the minister. I do not doubt his word at all, but personally I am not convinced. I think the drug manufacturers on this continent are too much concerned about profits and too little concerned about the health of the people, and that is why I do not feel like taking that statement at face value.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL HEALTH AND WELFARE
speechtext:
A United States senate committee made an exhaustive investigation into the drug traffic on this continent, and if hon. members care to take time they can go to the library in this building and read the report of that committee, together with the evidence presented before it. It is a most terrific indictment of the drug manufacturers of the continent of North America and of Great Britain.

speechtext: The house in committee of supply, Mr. Macdonald (Brantford City) in the chair.

Mr. Chairman, when the committee rose at six o'clock I was making some observations on the estimates of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and pointing out what I thought was neglect on the part of his department in not checking more carefully on a possible source of relief for persons suffering from arthritis. During the course of my remarks the minister stated that they had information from two sources- he named someone in the Soviet Union as one -to the effect that this particular drug known as ACS had no medical value.
When I first saw reference to this particular drug I did not consider that the statement had emanated from any propaganda source within the Soviet Union. I saw it in the May, 1944, issue of Magazine Digest in an article written by Paul Winterton, Moscow correspondent of the News Chronicle. The story he wrote at that time would lead one to believe that there was definite and positive hope for relief from the afflictions of arthritis, by the use of this particular drug.
I should like to repeat what I said before six o'clock. If the story in connection with that particular serum was merely propaganda, I should like to know it. I think the people of Canada who took that as a possible source of relief from that particular disability should have their minds disabused of any idea they may have that the government has neglected to take up something which might afford relief to those suffering from arthritis.
I want to tell the minister that I appreciate his difficulties. He is head of a new department and, as I stated before, he has a whole lot of stumbling blocks to get over, not the least of which is the British North America Act. I was in hopes that the dominion-provincial conference would have decided the field of jurisdiction in these matters. I am convinced that until such time as the federal government has the taxing powers necessary to finance and to a large extent administer an adequate social security scheme across this country we are not going to solve the problem we are discussing here to-night, the health of the people of Canada. I hope that before many years have passed the federal government will measure up to its responsibilities. As long as you keep passing the buck from the
Supply

Health and Welfare

federal to the provincial authorities you are not going to get anything done in connection with health matters. I want to know whether there is any possibility of relief for those suffering from arthritis.
There is another specific matter about which I should like the government to do something. When the Family Allowances Act was passed there was quite a lengthy discussion and the act was examined from all angles. I believe that was a step in the right direction because it has done a lot of good. However, in my opinion discrimination is being practised. When the bill was being discussed I asked the minister if it provided for payments to illegitimate children or other children being maintained in institutions, and the minister replied that in his opinion it did. But I now find that these allowances are not being paid to children maintained in institutions. If a child is either boarded out or adopted from an institution, its foster parents receive the family allowance. But the child who remains in the institution does not come within the scope of the Family Allowances Act. I contend that there is discrimination, because I understood that the act would be made applicable to every child born in Canada.
Illegitimacy is a social problem. A child unfortunate enough to be born under those circumstances should not be penalized for something for which he is not responsible. In looking over a recent isue of a very good paper, the Glace Bay Gazette-
Oh, oh.

It is a good paper. The mine workers happen to own it themselves. An editorial contained certain figures with respect to this matter and showed that there had been an increase during the war. I am not going to give the figures, but the fact is that illegitimacy during the war years was not as high as it was in 1936. When you refer to the war years people say, "Oh, yes, there was war hysteria; people were uprooted; nothing was normal and that is merely the effects of .a war." The fact that it was higher in 1936 than it was during the war is proof positive that the war was not responsible.
This is a permanent social evil within our structure of society. Either it must be removed or the victims of it treated the same as other citizens of the country. Many people are too prone to look with scorn upon the girl who happens to get herself into that situation. Anyone who has any idea of conditions in the slums of our cities will agree with me when I say that at least ninety-five per cent of the girls who fall victims to this kind [Mr. Gillis.)
of thing do so because they were brought up in homes that were totally inadequate. There was not sufficient income in the home to provide most of these girls with a decent dress to wear, and most of them were unemployed. They did not have a decent pair of stockings ' to put on. They could not afford recreation of any kind, and if they had a boy friend they could not take him home because in the majority of cases they were ashamed of their homes through no fault of their parents because the order of society under which they lived did not enable them to provide these modern necessities. So that when a girl becomes a victim she is obliged, despite the fact that we have all these hospitals and all the medical fraternity-
Has the hon. member any statistics to bear out his statement that these transgressors come mainly from the poor?
I did not say, from the poor.
From people who lived in poor houses and poor surroundings. I think the hon. member meant the poor in a broad sense.
I think eighty-five per cent of the people of this country can be considered poor, and these victims come largely from that section of society.	[DOT]
I do not like the indictment.
It is not an indictment at all. If they were not poor they would not go through the ordeal of having to go into a charitable institution.
I dispute that.

Those who have sufficient means can avoid the possibility of being exposed. There are ways and means, if you can pay for it, that will enable them to do that. The fact of the matter is that those who are obliged to go through that ordeal come from homes where there are not [DOT] sufficient funds to cover up the transgression.
As I was going on to say, despite the fact that we have all these hospitals and all this research in medical science, a well-organized medical fraternity and standard hospitals from coast to coast, as the minister pointed out, when one of these girls falls a victim, and a victim, I repeat, of a faulty order of society, she is obliged to seek refuge in a charitable institution. The charitable institution is not maintained for profit. It is operated in all cases by people who are interested in doing something for those who are not able to do for themselves. There is practically no com-

Supply-Health and Welfare
pensation for such people by way of salaries, and the institution is operated inadequately because of lack of funds.
Under the present scheme of things these institutions are the responsibility of the municipality and the province. The grants that are made by the municipalities are far too small. They have not the funds or the means of taxation to make large grants; and under the present set-up, where the federal government has invaded the fields of taxation of the province, the powers of the province to make adequate grants are restricted. Therefore we find these institutions operated on a charitable basis, and a large number of children are left in the institution because they cannot be boarded out. That is a burden which cannot be borne much longer by those who operate institutions of that kind. I have visited some of them and I know the terrific struggle they are making. I know that most of the doctors *who look after the patients in such institutions do it for nothing, and they should not have to. Practically no one connected with the institution receives anything by way of salary, and they all work long hours.
The time has come when the least the federal government can do, because this is a federal act and it is supposed to be applicable to all the children in Canada, and the federal government has the taxing powers necessary for the next eighteen months at least to collect the necessary funds, would be to make the act applicable to all children born in Canada. Despite the fact that for the past fifty or sixty years we have been trying to shift the responsibility from one to the other, the time has come when we must face realities, and I urge the minister to give reconsideration to living up to the statement that was made when the act was first brought down that the family allowance would apply to all children in Canada. The least that the federal government can do is to allow the five or six dollars for each child so that it may be properly fed and properly clothed and sent out in as healthy a state as possible. I do not think that is asking too much and I do not believe it would involve a large expenditure of money.
The minister may take the stand that these are private institutions. They are in a sense, but they were made'necessary because no other institution had been set up for the purpose of performing this function. They may be private, but they are not operated for a profit, and I think it would be carrying out an obligation on the part of the federal government as wall as a gesture of charity to extend the scope of the act to make it all-inclusive so far as the children in Canada are concerned.

I may be living in past days, but I am convinced that some of the best cures for disease are those that are plainest, cheapest and most easily understood. I think the minister will agree with me-I am judging by his conduct-that the best kind of cure for disease is plain food and lots of it, and the right kind of things to drink.
Somebody has said that a fence at the top of a hill is better than an ambulance down in the valley; and good plain food, as the minister has proven, is a splendid prevention against disease. The stand that he has taken in the family allowance which enables children to have plenty of good food and to be properly cared for is the best cure for arthritis and all allied diseases. I think the minister is going to ask his experts to spend a good deal of their time in finding the cause of arthritis, tuberculosis, cancer and other diseases.
There are some members of the house who will agree with me that one of the causes of sickness is overwork. There are men in this house who, in the eyes of some people outside, may not be doing much work but who, nevertheless, are broken through overwork in this house.
In order to get good food every home should have somebody that is a real honest breadwinner who works every day and he should see to it that the boys and girls with whom that, home has been blest go to bed in decent time and do not use the things that will hurt their health. Any athlete knows-dear knows, I know well-that no boy or girl can smoke cigarettes and take care of his eyes, his heart, his stomach, his nervous system. I am sure the minister will pay some attention to this menace in the future.
Smoking?

Preventives will be found in good food, lots of sleep and healthy exercise. May I say that there are some men in this house who would do well to take more healthy exercise and it is the duty of some of us to see that they get the opportunity. I hope that such opportunities will be available in future and that we shall enjoy recreation in a good, honest, humorous way.
I spent some time on a committee, trying to help the Minister of Veterans Affairs. It continued for two years, and experts were called from all over the world, from Australia, New Zealand, Great Britain, the United States and various parts of Canada. To-day we have a health insurance policy second to none in the world. It is on a contributory basis, and my attitude in that connection is that every man in health and strength who
________Sup-ply-Health and Welfare

has a job-and many times it is his own fault if he has not a job-should contribute to his own future. Quite a while ago a former minister of labour sponsored a scheme of annuities which was a splendid insurance policy; I know of nothing in Canada of this kind which can beat it. I am sure that as soon as possible the government will put contributory health insurance into operation.
The information I get from heads of homes is that the family allowance is proving most effective as a preventive of disease. From the point of view of nutrition, the Speaker of this house and the Sergeant-at-Arms know that a good drink of wholesome milk to growing boys in the afternoon is a valuable contribution to the upbuilding of their health. My purpose in speaking this evening is to urge the minister to put emphasis on measures of prevention rather than to try to pick people up from the bottom of the valley when they have fallen victims to overwork or disease.

Having listened this afternoon to the statement made by the Minister of National Health, I think it behooves me to commend him for having based himself on scientific and especially on medical data in the account he gave of what he has done. I feel quite justified in paying him such a compliment because I am dealing with a branch of social science with which I am acquainted when I speak about medicine. I have also had the pleasure, later in the afternoon, to hear some of our opponents, a few C.C.F. and Social Credit members speak on the subject of medicine when they questioned the minister's statements connected with arthritis and rheumatism. I noticed that the minister did not say much on these questions when our hon. friends across the floor went to a great deal of trouble in explaining to him that those diseases should be placed on the same basis as cancer and tuberculosis. I regret to say to my hon. friends, who refer to arthritis as being a disease, that they should consider it as a syndrome rather than a disease. When they urge the Minister of National Health to make treatment available for those who suffer from arthritis they might as well ask him to provide for the treatment of all common diseases. Arthritis is not a disease, but as I said, a combination of medical syndromes; when a physician examines a person who suffers from arthritis, he may discover various ailments such as cirrhosis, nephritis and other diseases. Having practised medicine during twenty-six years, I know the terrible suffering caused by cancer. I rose to-night simply to ask the

minister to do everything in his power so that every bit of scientific knowledge and research may be used in our fight against so terrible a lisease.
Secondly, there is tuberculosis. Its causes are now known and that is a step in the right direction. On the other hand, from a practical point of view, we know absolutely nothing about cancer. The work of research should be continued in both those fields.
I want to challenge a certain statement, made by an hon. member opposite, from the scientific point of view. A C.C.F. member told us that a certain Russian serum sent to Canada and which had given results in Russia was kept from the Canadian people. From the point of view of the Canadian medical fraternity generally, such a statement is absolutely without foundation. The Canadian Medical association, indeed the medical profession throughout the whole world, is much too honest, much too interested in the welfare of all human beings to hid from a single group or nation, a scientific discovery that might be a blessing to all mankind. I do not believe that there is anything to the rumour, and it is unbelievable that this Russian discovery if it has any merit would not be welcomed by the government and the Canadian medical profession.
I want the public to understand that whenever Canadian medical men have made a discovery, whether it be of little or of momentous importance, it has always been given to the world and used for the well-being of mankind. I could quote several instances, but it is sufficient to glance through newspapers, without delving into medical subjects, to find out that as soon as insulin had been discovered by a Canadian physician it was made available to the whole world. The same may be said of penicillin. Then, if I may mention something more personal, there is the case of my own father who discovered a new abdominal operating technique. After he had submitted his new technique to the Canadian medical profession, an Italian physician requested detailed information in respect thereof; the details of the new technique were forwarded to the Italian medical men who have made use of it for the greatest benefit to mankind.
Mr. Chairman, on behalf of Canadian medicine, of the whole Canadian medical profession, in fact, I wish to protest. There is not the slightest doubt that, had Russia discovered a product for the relief of the victims of arthritis, the Canadian government, and the Canadian medical profession, could not have rejected it. To claim otherwise is going entirely too far, and I refuse to believe it unless I am given the most convincing proofs.

Supply-Health and Welfare
I urge the Minister of National Health to help our rural population, especially in connection with hospitalization. The farmers' income is only sufficient to allow them to secure individual treatment from their family doctors, but it is inadequate to take care of hospitalization when needed. When an operation, a surgical intervention, is indicated, I ask the government to find some way of solving the problem of paying for hospitalization. Could not either the federal or the provincial authorities take care of this, I am not discussing the principle of this question; I am only pointing out the blunt fact that our farmers cannot afford to pay for hospitalization when an operation is needed. I ask the Minister of National Health to give them efficient help in cases of this kind.
In concluding, I wish to offer a suggestion. Preventive medicine is infinitely superior to curative treatments. The minister should give special attention to popular education in medical matters. Results are invariably better achieved through persuasion and conviction than through coercion and legislative action. The government should place in the hands of public organizations the means of educating the masses. Our citizens must be told that periodic examinations are essential. We should teach our people that every Canadian should pay a periodic visit to his physician, as some insurance companies require of their policyholders, who must be examined every year or every five years as prescribed by them. This way it is easier to discover certain diseases which would otherwise remain unknown until too late. Again I say, prevention is better than cure.

This afternoon we had a most interesting discussion which to my mind has brought out two points of view. First of all, so many members have mentioned the pressing need for research into arthritis and cancer and have addressed their remarks to the minister that it would appear that many persons in the house and in Canada think this department is the one that should do medical research. Of course, I join with those members who have spoken in agreeing that medical research into such diseases as arthritis and cancer is of the utmost importance and is a matter upon which money can be well spent, but it is apparent from what the minister has said that any moneys which might be expended on such matters do not come within this vote.
I want to turn the discussion to something which arises when one discusses estimates, and that is the question whether expenditures are proper or not. It seems to me that we have to balance the urgent demand for the spending of larger sums against the almost equally
urgent demand for the elimination of unnecessary expenditures and therefore for the reduction in taxation which would then be possible.
Thinking that over, it struck me that these two points of view can be reconciled only if one determines that for any money that is voted value is obtained. That is how I proprose to approach the estimates. I want to make a few observations in particular about the estimates other than the statutory vote. Of the amount of about $11,000,000, $5,500,000 is referable to Indian affairs and the national film board, which hardly arise in this discussion. They are, I think, separate items. That leaves $5,500,000 being voted for national health and welfare, and I think the Canadian people would have believed that in that $5,500,000 there would be something for medical research, whereas in fact there is not.
The whole vote seems to be made up of three items: administration of certain statutes which come under the purview of the minister, such as immigration medical service, quarantine, leprosy and the Proprietary and Patent Medicines Act; social welfare generally, not in the field of research; and the item of publicity. Of that item of $5,500,000 of which I speak, roughly ten per cent is taken up in votes for publicity. I wish to lay before the committee what those particular votes are, because I am going to argue that while, of course, publicity has its proper place in the expenditures of this department, the amount for that purpose is so large that this money might very well either not be voted or, if voted to the department, be put to much better use so that we would get more value for what we spend, and thus the two points of view I mentioned at first might be reconciled.
Going through the estimates, I find that this year departmental administration gets an allotment of $50,000 for publicity. There is no change from last year and it represents no less than twelve per cent of the total expenditures on departmental administration. Turning to the health branch, I find that the administration of that branch is given $100,000 for publicity. That is no less than 50 per cent of the total vote to that particular branch and represents an increase of $80,000 in the publicity item. It is up five times. The third item, child and maternal hygiene, is $68,400, or 60 per cent of the total for that special department. The next subdivision is public health engineering, which has never had a vote before for publicity so far as I can find out. It is now granted $30,000 for publicity, which is 20 per cent of its total vote. Industrial hygiene is allotted $21,000 for publicity, or 20 per cent of its total vote. The civil service health division
Supply-Health and Welfare

is granted 118,000 for publicity, which represents 10 per cent of its total vote. That item is down from last year. The nutrition service subdivision is granted $50,000 for publicity. That sum represents 28 per cent of its total vote. Venereal disease control is granted $5,000 for publicity, which represents 12 per cent of its total vote. The directorate of health insurance studies is granted $3,500 for publicity, which is eight per cent of all that goes to it.
Then we come to the dental health division which is granted $30,000 for publicity. This vote is up $28,000 from last year. The amount this year represent 50 per cent of the total vote for that branch. The same can be said of the mental health division. It receives $5,000 for publicity, which represents 20 per cent of the total vote for the branch. The blindness control division is given a small vote of $500. The percentage is negligible and I shall not quote it. The tuberculosis control division is granted $5,000 for publicity, which again represents 20 per cent of its total vote. The advertising and labels division gets $1,200 for publicity. That again is a small proportion of the total vote, and I have not the percentage figure. The Indian medical service receives a new vote of $10,000 for publicity. We shall deal with this when we come to the item, but it can be said that it is a little strange that medical assistance to Indians should require any vote for publicity.
I turn now to the welfare branch and we come first of all to branch administration. This branch gets $4,000 for publicity, or nine per cent of its total vote. The family allowances division gets $150,000 for publicity purposes this year, the same amount as last year. This is seven per cent of the total administrative expenses of the Family Allowances Act. The old age pensions division gets no grant for publicitjr. The national physical fitness administration is allowed $18,930 for publicity, which is a large percentage, namely 37 per cent, of its total vote. The total of all the items I have read out is $570,530. Over half a million dollars is being spent on publicity and advertising by this department out of a total vote of $5,500,000. Last year only $416,000 was spent on advertising and publicity. Therefore the total vote for that purpose is up $154,000 this year when, in my view, we should be doing everything we can to curtail expenditures.
The two other general observations I wish to make about the publicity vote are as follows. In the first place, this department has the second largest allotment for publicity of any department of government. It is ex-
'
ceeded only by the Department of Trade and Commerce. The other notable thing is that as one searches through the estimates one finds that very few of the subdivisions of the uepartment failed to put in a bid1 for their quota of this publicity vote.
If we turn to the department in its infancy we find that in the first annual report of the department for the year ended March 31, 1945, the total amount spent by the minister's department upon publicity was $165,570; quite a different sum from $570,000 this year. Of that total of two years ago, no less than $115,000 was spent in the control of venereal disease, whereas this year that vote for publicity is down to $5,000. Therefore we can see a tremendous and alarming increase of expenditures in respect of publicity in this department.
Before continuing on this question of publicity, may I say that the other interesting thing that arose this afternoon appeared in the statement made by the minister in which he outlined that he believed to be the proper scope of his department. Since he said that it was a new department last year and only just formed and in operation, I think it would be most interesting to all members of the committee if during this discussion the minister stated further what he believes to be the proper scope of the activities of the department. This afternoon he said that he believed the dominion government should assist programmes of research, and that research was carried on through the national research council. Naturally I agree with that statement of policy, but I believe that the people of Canada would have thought that the Department of National Health and Welfare, which is spending a large sum of money this year, would have had that task included in its vote. We should hear from the minister as to how the activities of the national research council and medical research are coordinated; whether the minister has any right to direct what research shall be conducted and any power of controlling or augmenting the funds which are granted to the national research council for medical research.
Since, however, medical research is not in his department I wish to continue with this matter of publicity and to ask the minister if he will give us his views upon the proper place of publicity in his department. I shall offer a few suggestions of my own before I sit down. It is my view that publicity certainly has its place, and in the course of my remarks I shall indicate one place where I think it is properly expended. But publicity

Supply-Health and Welfare
is a dangerous thing to play with. In my opinion it must be strictly governed by the test that I suggested, namely, value for money.
I would ask the minister, as we come to these votes for publicity, to explain in each case what degree of efficiency he believes arises out of these grants for publicity purposes, and also if he does not think he would get more value in relation to the health of the Canadian people if he spent some of these funds in other ways. For instance, the hon. member for Lanark has brought up the need for money grants to aid in neurosurgery research in Montreal, and certainly we have heard enough about arthritis and cancer to make us realize that grants to bodies conducting that kind of research would be money well spent. So I say to the minister that in my view, particularly at a time when we need to review our expenditures, it is not sufficient to point out what is undoubtedly true, that from all the money spent on publicity some benefit will be realized. Rather he must go further, I suggest, and show that great benefit will be realized, greater benefit than would result if the money were applied elsewhere.
I wish to make one or two other observations on the matter of publicity, taking a very broad view. In the first place, as the minister has said, health and welfare is a provincial matter. I should like to hear from him what is the tie-up, in the expenditure of money for disseminating to the Canadian people information on public health and welfare, with each of the provinces. How are these expenditures coordinated with those of the provinces, to be sure that they are not advertising the same thing or perhaps even a slightly different thing, and that there is no duplication or overlapping in these expenditures? The second broad observation I would make is that direct advertising to the public is rather by-passing provincial health authorities, who have trained staffs in the field, and to me would seem prima facie to be not making the best use of this money which, if it is to be spent on publicity purposes, might be better spent by way of grants to the provinces for these purposes instead of indirect action by this government.
My next general observation is that I believe the percentage effect of advertising is probably remarkably low. In order that one may get the best results, surely one should particularize in one's advertising rather than generalize. To give a specific example, I want to point out that the sum of $68,000 is allotted for publicity in respect of child
and maternal care. It is my understanding that the booklet which probably represents most of that money is very useful indeed, and that it is doing a great deal of good in the field of child and maternal care in this country. That is the sort of advertising. which one can readily approve, where there is a clear need by an obvious class, and where it is almost certain that this class will be only too anxious to read and study and apply that publicity. On the other hand, as I understand it, the department gets out another booklet called the "Master Menu Pattern", which, if you please, is a bright little document telling the p'eople of Canada what food to take with them when they go on picnics in the summer, and how best to make use of that food. I have no hesitation whatever in saying that, in my view, money spent on the "Master Menu Pattern" is absolutely and completely wasted. I believe any persons in this country who go on a picnic know enough to take with them the food they want to eat, rather than the food described in such a booklet. That, I say. breaks a good rule of advertising, because it is offered to the Canadian people as a whole, while there is no demand for it and it is probably not read. In the army we had a "paper war", antf we know what we did with pieces of paper like this.
I want to give one further illustration of this generality that may destroy the usefulness of expenditures of this kind. I refer now to what I call paternalism in advertising, telling the Canadian people, in terms which a very simple-minded man could understand, just what they ought to do. In this connection I wish to read what is called a "filler", issued by the division of information services of this department. I believe it is issued to the newspapers, and it says it may be used at any time. It states:
Just because people have reached middle age, they should not give up all forms of exercise, say health authorities. An official of the Department of National Health and Welfare, Ottawa, states: "There is no reason why a person in the prime of life should abandon health-giving exercise. In fact, the evidence is all in favour of recreation at all ages. Of course, the family physician should be consulted, so that all may keep fit without strain at this most important time of life."
I do not know how much a filler costs, but I do say that this is paternalism in its worst form. Instead of promoting the health of this country, a thing like that is debilitating to the morale and to the mind; and I do not think any money spent on that sort of thing is well spent. In the first place, it is the most enormous platitude, and that is the best thing you can say for it. Another thing
Supply-Health and Welfare

one could say, I suppose, is that it is a most outrageous blurb. There are more of these "fillers" which we can dish out during consideration of the estimates.
Another point I wish to make in connection with this question of publicity is that there is great danger of duplication. For instance, I have here in a file a calendar put out by the magazine Health, which tells you what you should eat every day. It gives you the right menu for Monday, for Tuesday, and so on. It is a very good thing, I am sure, but 1 think every hon. member knows that over a period of many years various magazines and periodicals have put out so many of these things, which are mutually contradictory, that adding one more to the lot will not make any difference.
The same thing might be said about the publication, "Canadian Health and Welfare Bulletin" put out by the department. I understand that this is printed, 50,000 copies in English and 25,000 copies in French, and is distributed free. I am sure all hon. members get a copy; I know I do. Just before these estimates were presented I got one and I read it. I also get a copy of the magazine Health, put out by a private organization which, I believe, receives some financial assistance under these votes.
Two of these magazines are unnecessary. Everything that goes into the departmental magazine could go into the other. The circulation of the departmental magazine could easily be added to the circulation of the private magazine, if there is not already duplication. The Department of National Health and Welfare should not be a printing and publishing office; it should be a Department of National Health and Welfare.
These are all the general observations I want to make, but there are some questions I should like to ask about vote 200, departmental administration. I wish the minister were in the chamber at the moment.
