speechtext: He will be back at once.
I think I shall wait until the minister returns.

I have listened quite attentively to the speeches of the hon. members for Lanark, Peace River, Weyburn and others, who have preceded me and I have found them most interesting. After hearing the views of those hon. members, I must say that I agree with those who feel that we should spend for protecting the health of Canadians as much if not more than we have spent for sending them to war.

However, while physical health is important, I believe that the spiritual sphere, which is still more important, should not be neglected. As an old latin proverb says: "Mens sana in corpore sano." That is why I claim that the primary duty of a government anxious to protect the true interests of the people, is to give them servants who respect and elevate them instead of degrading and debasing them. Doctor Chisholm, deputy minister of health, who is unable to distinguish between good and evil, does not deserve his present position and he should be replaced by some one intelligent enough to respect the faith of those who believe in God. It is a disgrace that we should have civil servants as devoid of moral principles as Doctor Chisholm and we should not hesitate, through decency and concern for public morals, to dismiss him so as to prevent him from spreading throughout Canada, with the government's approval, his subversive ideas and from flaunting his atheism. It is high time that consideration be given to the numerous petitions to the government requesting the resignation of Doctor Chisholm whose utterances are an insult to the decent citizens of this country.
No one can take as a pretext for avoiding action in this matter, the failure of the dominion-provincial conference. Let us dismiss General Chisholm and replace him by some one competent in the field of moral health as well as in those of physical health or social welfare. I think that such a reform is the one that is most urgent in the Department of National Health and Welfare, and I am sure that a considerable part of the population would be quite pleased if the minister complied with the requests that have recently been directed to him in this connection.

In order to relieve my rather solemn talk I should like to read another of these fillers. It reads:
Now is the time to substitute the fruit bowl for the cookie jar in Canadian kitchens, say Ottawa health authorities.
While the minister was out of the chamber I made some general observations with respect to the expenditure of money by his department for publicity purposes. It. will be noted that there is one item for $50,000 covering publicity and information. Then under the health branch there is another vote of $100,000 for publicity and information, and later on there is still another vote for $4,000. The total amount voted for publicity in connection with the administrative branches of the Department of National Health and Welfare is $154,000. Incidentally, that is the exact amount of the increase this year in connection with

Supply-Health and Welfare
publicity. All other votes for publicity in connection with specific items for specific branches are in addition to this $154,000.
I consider that the members of this committee would be more prepared to approve these votes for publicity if they were earmarked specifically for definite purposes rather than being voted for general publicity purposes. For example, I think it would be better to increase the amount expended on publicity in connection with child and maternal hygiene and decrease the main vote by that much.
I am wondering if this $50,000 we are talking about would not be better spent if it were in the form of grants to organizations now covered by votes 233 to 242. These cover giants to the Canadian Welfare council; to the Canadian Red Cross society, which gets only $10,000; to the St. John Ambulance association, which gets only $4,050, and other grants. This money could also be used to good purpose to support some of the institutions mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for Lanark.
In the light of the remarks I have made I should like to ask some specific questions about this item of $50,000 in vote 200. First, how was the similar vote of $50,000 expended last year? I should like that answered in some detail. I should like also if the minister could explain to the committee just what is the division of information services mentioned in the annual report of the department, and how it works.
Second, I should like to know how it is proposed to spend the $50,000 to be allotted this year. Upon what principles are these disbursements made? Is it under a scheme now laid down by the minister to attain specific purposes which he has in mind; or alternatively is it a reservoir into which all the departments may dip if they find they have exhausted the publicity vote specifically allotted to them; or alternatively again is it a fund available to publicize some new idea to be born in the department during the year but which has not yet been conceived?
Finally, is the expenditure of this money coordinated with provincial departments to prevent overlapping? I shall be glad to ask these questions, of which I know there are quite a number, individually, if the minister prefers.
Mr. LaCROIX: Are there any possibilities of securing bilingual forms in connection with the family allowances? Are they at the disposal of the public in different provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
In every family allowance office,-and there is one in each province,-
forms are available in English and in French and correspondence is carried on in both English and French. So far as we can do it, we make the application forms for the family allowance available in both English and French in all the offices and in all the post offices, which is the other source from which the application forms can be got. Anyone can write in to the family allowance office for his province in French or in English and be replied to in the language in which he corresponds and receive a form in the language in which he wants to fill out his application.
Mr. LaCROIX: Does that apply to all the provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: Yes.
Would the minister now answer my questions?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has raised quite a few questions about publicity in connection with the administration of this department. In the first place, it should be said that the estimates are the amounts which the officers of the department who are experienced in such matters, after having consulted with their advisers, consider necessary to cover the field adequately. When these have been passed through the department and verified by the department, they appear as items in the estimates. This does not mean that the amount asked for will be spent in every case, but if we take publicity, for example, it means that in every case there is a programme of publicity designed or in course of preparation which would use some such amount if it is desirable to spend the money.
The work of public health is one which must be carried on a number of fronts at once. First, there is the devoted work of doctors and nurses; second, the provision of adequate facilities for treatment and care, hospitals and laboratories; third, the work of scientists and doctors in research; fourth, the work of public health authorities, provincial and municipal, supplemented by the federal; fifth, and perhaps most important of all, the work of public education.
The real gap in our performance, either as federal health authorities, provincial health authorities or municipal or voluntary health authorities, is not in our knowledge but in the difference between what we know and what we do. We now know enough about disease to wipe out most of the killing power of most diseases from which men suffer except cancer and arthritis. But tuberculosis and a great many other diseases could be wiped out
Supply-Health and Weljare

completely with the knowledge we have. The difference between what we do and what we know is due just to the failure of public opinion to support the demands of health authorities and others for adequate assistance and adequate support. We must bring home to the people the fact that they can secure adequate help and assistance if they go to the doctor, take his advice and follow it soon enough. That is true also of the killer, cancer. So that I would say that to-day the greatest single failure of public health authorities is a lack of education and a lack of information. If we are to do anything in this field to bring what we know we can do up so as to match what we should do, that gap must be bridged by public information.
One of the most interesting things in this field is the demonstration given by the Metropolitan Life Insurance company over a great number of years. As far back as 1912 that company found that it was beginning to have interesting experiences in connection with public health education, so that instead of advertising insurance it advertised health. It has carried on that service ever since at great expense but at great profit, because its statistics show that there is a consistent difference between the records of the people to whom the advertisements have been directed and to whom its health service has been offered and the records of the rest of the population. It has shown the way in institutional advertising of that kind.
We are not going in for anything like that. The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard has picked out the items and said that they represent about ten per cent of the controllable items in the total vote for this department. I am not sure about his figures, but I imagine that he has given the correct amount -ten per cent for education. I think that is a pretty fair figure. But I must say that we had it in mind that it was desirable to use a much bigger figure. There is a good deal to be said on either side about every advertisement.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard was good enough to refer with commendation to the pamphlet "Mother and Child", of which more than a million copies have been circulated in Canada free. It has probably the greatest circulation of any single Canadian book except the bible. It was written by Doctor Couture for the department and widely circulated in both languages. Since that book has been distributed, infant and maternal mortality rates in Canada have improved. We do not claim credit for the improvement, but we do say that you cannot

have improvement unless people know what should be done. The greatest thing that should be done in most of these fields is to see the doctor in time and to follow his advice.
The hon. member has asked me to say how much of this programme has been discussed with the provinces. A very considerable amount of it has been, through an agency known as the Dominion Council of Health, which meets twice a year, where representatives of the provinces, the dominion and the public meet together for three or four days and decide on programmes, and a very considerable proportion of this has been discussed by them. There is always a danger in saying how much a province has approved a thing, because some time later it may turn out that the required authority was not forthcoming from the province to give the appropriate blessing to that particular project. All we can; do is consult with the officials and the ministers who are willing to consult with us. We have done that on every possible occasion; and I can assure the committee that the demands for expenditures by the dominion coming from the provinces are far greater than the expenditures we are providing for in these estimates.
Let us look at just one other possible^ comparison in this field. Perhaps it may not be so relevant; but if there is anything in the assertion I make that public information and education are important in the realm of health, then how important is it? Is it as important as advertising this particular brand or that particular commodity? The amount, if the total the hon. member says is right, as I assume it is, which we ask here as a possible expenditure would, I should think, judging from my experience in these matters, be a good deal less than half that sought for . the advertising of particular commodities by half a dozen or more Canadian industries. We believe that these expenditures pay dividends just as industrialists believe that their expenditures pay. We believe that these expenditures have paid dividends in the past. I can remember when tuberculosis caused the deaths of 200 out of' 100,000 Canadians, and I went as a small boy to the first antituberculosis exhibition in Canada, on Ontario street in Montreal. It was one of the first in the world, and was the beginning of a campaign of education, and from that campaign -has been produced the result that in forty years we have eradicated three-fourths of the former killing power of tuberculosis in Canada. I believe that we can do the same thing with other diseases and conditions, taking

Supply-Health and Welfare
them one after another, and that also in the fields of nutrition and positive health and preventive medicine we can achieve still more.
With regard to the items for publicity, I would be glad to go into them if the hon. member wants to raise each one as it comes along. I would, however, ask him and the committee to consider that in working out the affairs of a department like this we are still understaffed; we have to do what we can with the people we can get, and we can lay out a programme and then find that it coincides with a victory loan or some other major national advertising campaign, so that it has to be postponed or dropped. It requires a good deal of flexibility in the arrangement of these things to make the most effective use of the money. I think we have done that. I have never 'heard any suggestion that any of the money was used for improper purposes.
The hon. member questioned this pamphlet about camping. We can show, for his testimony, I suppose, a hundred letters saying that it is a very good thing and asking for more copies. There are two opinions on most of these questions of publicity, but there are no two opinions, as I think the hon. member would be one of the first to agree, about the necessity for public education and publicity and information in the field of health. I respectfully represent to the committee that the total amount sought is not too large, having regard to the fact that some of these matters must be dealt with on a nation-wide basis if they are to have any effect. We endeavour to cooperate with the provinces and local agencies in every way we can; we will do the best we can with the money parliament allows us, and I believe it will pay dividends in the health of the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there are a few words I should like to add to the discussion of this important matter. I regard as a very good sign the extent to which it has been argued by almost everyone who has taken part in the debate to-day that the health of our people should be a major concern of government. At times we hear theoretical arguments about the place of government in a democracy, and in such arguments there are those who contend that governments should interfere as little as possible with the affairs of the people. It is my view, however-and I think that view has been expressed by all who have spoken to-day -that in reality government is the collective effort of people in a democracy to make their own lives better and happier in every possible
way; and I suggest that there is no sphere of our human activity in which more can be done toward achieving that ideal than in the sphere of health. I hope we may look forward in the years that lie ahead in Canada to an increasing part being played by governments in helping to improve the health of our people.
I had thought to make some comments on the criticisms levelled at the expense of information and publicity by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard; but perhaps the minister has already given an answer which, I am sure, will carry weight with the hon. member who made the criticisms. After all, what we need is not less information but more of it. It is still true that the truth can help to make us free from a good many diseases and1 other afflictions of human life.
I should like to say a word about a subject which was before us a good deal this afternoon, that of research into a number of different diseases. I want to support those who have pleaded with the minister for all the assistance the government can give to research in connection with cancer, arthritis and other ailments which have been mentioned to-day. The minister, in replying, told us of the way in which the government prefers to carry on its research in the medical field, that is by having it done through a committee of the national research council on which this department is represented, and I think most hon. members who have spoken agreed that that is the better way to do it. But sometimes wTe find, in dealing with governments, that when two bodies are concerned with the same matter there is a little tendency to "buck-passing"; and my only hope is that having this way of doing it will not be an excuse for the minimum amount being done.
I was glad to hear the minister suggest that in the matter of public information and education he had tried to get more from the treasury board than they were prepared to grant. I hope that in this matter of medical research, if it is left to a committee of the national research council he will fight with all the vigour he has and instruct the members of his department to do likewise, to ensure that just as much as possible can be done, and not simply the minimum, in this field.
In connection with medical research, there is this point I would ask him to consider, that it be not done only in laboratories. As hon. members know, only two days ago I was myself a patient in an institution in this country which is quite famous. As a matter of fact it is located in the minister's constituency. I refer to the Montreal neurological institute
Supply-Health and Welfare

which has a considerable reputation not only throughout Canada but in all parts of the world. One of the main reasons for the fame of that institution is that it is not merely a hospital or merely a laboratory, but an institution in which the two are combined. We have there an eight-floor building, four floors of hospital and four floors of laboratory and experimental work, and it was my privilege, while there, to be not only a patient in bed, but, as a friend of some of the doctors, to get around and learn something of the work that is done in that institution. It was impressed upon me how valuable it is, in research into the kind of questions with which that institution is concerned, to have patients of all types and for the doctors and fellows by whom research is being carried on to have a chance to see not only the things in the test-tubes upstairs but the patients downstairs as well.
That raises the whole question as to whether there should not be some way whereby the government might make a grant not only for research in the laboratories but for the hospital side of an institution such as that, so that they can have patients who will enable those working there to do the best kind of research possible. I learned, while there, of the plea that Doctor Penfield, the superintendent, has been making for money, terribly small amounts of money, so that they may be able to minister to the needs of people who go there from all parts of Canada, and may be able to do research not only in some of the diseases mentioned to-day but in some others of a neurological nature, which also afflict a great many people in Canada. I do not expect the minister, since we have the estimates before us-and that is usually what passes in this house-to come back, before his department is through, with a promise of something else. I do ask him, however, to give consideration to this phase of research, namely, that it shall include not only the laboratory but the clinical side as well.
I would be remiss in my duty as one who feels a considerable debt of gratitude to the institution from which I have just come if I did not take this opportunity of stating that their position should be considered by the government. The institution is located in a city, in one of the provinces, and it receives some help from that city and that province; but it serves the whole of Canada and, indeed, has spread the name of Canada throughout the world because of the kind of work done there. I know the minister concurs in what I am saying about that institution, and I hope that consideration will be given to its needs, for the relief of human suffering, relief that might

result from the expenditure of a very few thousand dollars in further research in the institution. The institution is already there and has its equipment; its need is sufficient money to make full use of it.
There are one or two other thoughts I would leave with the minister. When we-speak in terms of national health, for the most part we think of-curative and corrective measures, of hospitals and treatment. Yet we have come to realize in this day and age that preventive measures are of equal importance. I am not by any means a faddist in matters of this kind. In fact, in regard to what I am about to say, I realize that I have perhaps broken my own rule thousands of times. However, I am convinced that medical and scientific men have not yet scratched the surface of the whole question of nutrition and its effect in building sound health. I suggest that it should be the concern of government, which is the collective effort of the people of a democracy to make their own lives better, to do some real research in this whole field of proper foods. As has been said by others, the objective should be to make it possible for th,e people to get proper foods so that we might build up, in a generation or two, a healthier Canadian nation than we have so far known, and one that might not be prone to many of the ills that we have been discussing this afternoon and evening. This is one of the reasons, I confess, I did not follow very closely the thinking of the member for Vancouver-Burrard; for here is a field where, instead of laughing at the few suggestions that have been made with regard to balanced diets, we should encourage the government to go much farther in providing for 'research and information so that our people might take the lead in building health through proper diet and nutrition.
One other thought and I will conclude. I was interested in reading the remarks of the minister on behalf of Canada at the economic and social council of the united nations with respect to organizing the health of the world. As I read his remarks I was proud that he had taken the aggressive position that he did. It is important that we concern ourselves with the health not only of our own back yard but of the whole community and of the whole world. There is no freedom from disease for any of us until we rid the world of disease, and so I was proud of the aggressive stand which the minister took on behalf of Canada. I do not wish to detract from that compliment-I mean it- but it seemed to me that it was a different person who stood up in the house this afternoon and defended the government for not

Supply-Health and Welfare
going farther and not acceding to the various requests made aggressively from this side during this debate. I would urge that the next time the minister appears in a meeting of the cabinet or of the treasury board in connection with these matters, he take on, not the character of one defending low expenditures. as he did this afternoon in defending failure to do this, that and the other * thing, but rather the character that he had when he spoke at the economic and social council. I would ask him to get in there and fight for the very best and the most aggressive programme for public health which it is possible for us to achieve.

I do not want to be unpopular with the hon. member or with any other hon. members to my left, nor do I wish to be too persistent in bothering the minister and his staff. I wish to say, however, that when I spoke of expenditures with regard to publicity and information, obviously a proper field for his department, all I asked was that we should have proof that we were going to get value for our money. I do not think that the simple spending of money in this department will necessarily bring the wonderful things about which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre spoke. It must go to the right place. One of the right places is the institute in Montreal which he mentioned, but that is by the way. My specific question to the minister was on this vote of $50,000. Y ould he say whether that money will be spent under a scheme now laid down by him to achieve certain purposes? If so, what are these purposes? Or is it a general reservoir into which these sub-departments may dip if they run beyond their own particular publicity vote?

I am going to suggest to the minister a way in which this question could be answered. This vote is the same as the one we had last year. If the minister will give us a break-down of last year's vote, then I think we shall have the information that the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard is seeking.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
The expenditure out of the vote of $50,000 which was provided last year is not yet available to me here for the year ended March 31, 1946. I might say that the expenditures to December 31, 1945, which is the last figure I have here, were $2,421.71. That left a considerable amount to be expended out of this vote. I think I can tell the hon. member that this vote is not earmarked for any particular purpose. It is there to be used for purposes which do not fall under any of the specific votes, but
are of such a nature that they apply to the department generally. The fact that the amount is set out does not, of course, mean that it will be fully spent. I think that gives the hon. member the answer he wants.

I have a question arising out of the answer just given. In view of the duty that is laid on the department to carry on the function of education and of the fact that an appropriation of $50,000 was provided last fall for that purpose, -what reason is to be given to the committee for the fact that only $2,400 has been spent on this important work?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: On what side of this question are my hon. friend and his party?

I agree with the minister in his remark this evening that our greatest problem is one of education. Where education is at its lowest ebb we have some of the worst records of health, and that bears out what he said. Where there is ignorance* we have fear, and where we have knowledge a lot of that fear disappears. There cannot be healthy people when the people are filled with fear. I recognize some of the difficulties of the minister in the operation of his department when there are nine provinces in each of which there is a department of health, and then more or less over and above these is the federal department. Would the minister explain how he decides how far his services shall go within each province? How does he spread his services? Does he spread the services in each province according to its need or according to the requests that have come in from the provincial governments, or does he carry on a sort of over-all service available to the provinces if and when they want it?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I am afraid it would have to depend on the kind of service that was considered. If it were in connection with venereal disease control, then there is provision for the allocation of money and medicines on an agreed basis with the provinces.
How about your staff?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
If it is staff, then the family allowances staff, for example, is the staff which is necessary to do the job within each province. With regard to food and drugs laboratories, and inspection, the staff is located at points where they can do the job best through the country without regard to provincial boundaries. Apart from these two, we have not any staffs generally scattered through the country.
Supply-Health and Welfare

I wondered, because I noticed that outside of the welfare branch, which I presume is doing most of the work with regard to the family allowances, the health branch have some 197 of a staff on a temporary and permanent basis, exclusive of Ottawa. The department has seen fit to put one temporary member of the staff in Saskatchewan. I did not hear Alberta complaining of the fact that they have only four. I could not understand why it was that the staff had been spread in a somewhat inequitable way.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: These would be food and drug inspectors.
They do not require them in Saskatchewan? Is that the idea?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It is generally related to the population and activities of various kinds in the provinces, particularly in centres where food is manufactured and distributed. If the hon. member assures me that there is one in Saskatchewan I will take his word for it.
I have the department's report.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: I would not think there would be more than one there.

In your own report, which was issued this year, there appears at page 73 a list of the health branches in the various provinces. This shows that Nova Scotia has a total of sixty-four employes; Manitoba, twelve; British Columbia, forty-seven; New Brunswick, twenty-two, and Quebec, twenty-eight. They are spread out in that way, and it does seem rather inequitable, not that I am finding a . great deal of fault with the minister; but if he is carrying on separate services with regard to laboratory work and drugs, finding out whether drugs and medicines are up to standard or whether these people are working in connection with the provincial governments on their educational work or whether it is a matter of seeing that the physical fitness programme is being carried on in the provinces, or whatever the function is, then there should be a more equitable distribution.
There is the problem of industrial diseases. Of course, that does not affect Saskatchewan to the same extent as it does others, but there must be the same problem of nutrition and the educational work that is to be carried on should be required there. I suggest that the department should have someone there keeping in contact with what the province is doing. Saskatchewan has an ambitious programme of health. They are taking the lead

in the Dominion of Canada. At the present time the government is providing free medical services, free hospitalization, free medicine, and, where required and recommended by the medical men, free dental care for 25,000 people in the province who are old age pensioners or dependent under the children's allowance act of the province. If the present plans of the province materialize, for a small fee they are going to be given to every person, young or old, rich or poor in the province. I think that is something to which the present department of health could give a good deal of assistance in the way of advertising to show the people of Canada what can be done.
The other question that I wanted to ask the minister perhaps should be brought up under one of these other items. That is, among the important features of any health scheme are the medical men and social service workers and those who carry on the educational work, particularly in the preventive field. In that connection I was just wondering whether the minister could tell us if any encouragement is given in regard to the training of medical men throughout Canada. During the war special grants were made, I believe through the Department of Labour, for the training of these people. In peace time we still require these medical men; Canada is still short of trained people in these fields, particularly in the field of preventive medicine. We are looking forward to the day when we shall be paying our medical men to keep the people of Canada well, and when we shall give them proper remuneration for that work. Those of us who lived on the western prairies during the hard years of the drought saw the medical men doing splendid work, giving everything they had and getting very little for it. The idea of paying our medical men to keep us well seems to me a much sounder principle than to have people who become ill unable to pay their medical men and feel themselves not in a position to call them. Would it not be much better for every person to know that whenever they become ill they may call in the doctor and receive proper hospital and medical treatment irrespective of their ability to pay at the time? Very often the poorest families are the largest, and that is where care is needed and where we find the least money per capita being spent on the service most required. If the minister is aiming to establish a healthy Canada, it seems to me he will have to face that problem, of setting up within this country a form of state medicine under which our medical people will be paid to keep us well.

Supply-Health and Weljare
Some of the figures across Canada in regard to certain diseases are alarming. Already in this debate statements have been made concerning health conditions among our Indians. When I think of some of the treaties that were signed with our red brothers, in which we said we would take care of them; then when I read some of the records in regard to the deathrate per 100,000 of population from tuberculosis in the various provinces, I hang my head in shame when I reflect what these people must think of those who made such promises to their forebears. For instance, I see that in Manitoba the death rate from tuberculosis is 1,421 per 100.000 among the Indians as compared with twenty-four among the white people. In Alberta it is 1.249-7 as compared with eighteen among the white people. The rate for all Canada is 757 among the Indians and forty-five among the white people.	-
The infant mortality rates in Canada, too, are such that we should hang our heads in shame. I notice that in some of the eastern provinces the rates are very high; and if this department is going to carry on an educational programme to better that condition, I should be quite satisfied to see only one of the minister's representatives in Saskatchewan and all the rest distributed throughout the other provinces where they are needed to carry on this work. The province of Alberta has, I think, four representatives of this department of the 197 in Canada outside of Ottawa. The infant mortality rates reveal that the figures for Quebec city are something like three times as high as those for some other cities. According to the report of the department, the rate in Vancouver and Calgary was twenty-nine, and it goes up from that figure as you go across Canada, taking in Hamilton, Victoria, London, Toronto, Saskatoon, Halifax, Ottawa, Regina and Windsor, where the rate is forty-six. The figure for Saint John, New Brunswick, is fifty; for Winnipeg, fifty-two; for Montreal and Verdun, sixty-one; for Three Rivers, seventy-one and for Quebec city, 104. Surely some big problem is involved there which will have to be faced, and I hope that in the course of his remarks the minister will inform the committee as to what plans he has in mind to deal with this situation.

Last evening, Mr. Chairman, I ventured several observations, to which the minister replied. If I may do so without wearying the committee I wish to go back to one or two of those matters, because in the
course of the last few minutes I think we have had light thrown on the answers given me by the minister last night.
First, I suggested that there was a distinct lack of information in the estimates as they have been laid before the house. I pointed out that we do not have before us the actual expenditures for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1946, at a time when we are being asked to approve estimates amounting to tremendous sums of money. Last evening I was told by the minister that the information would be forthcoming in due course in the public accounts. How many months must pass before the public accounts will be available we do not know, but certainly it will be long after the estimates now before the committee are disposed of. The public accounts will not be of the slightest assistance to us in reviewing the estimates now before us.
This evening we have dealt with one aspect of the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare, namely the expenditure on publicity and information. The hon, member for Vancouver-Burrard has pointed out that this item holds such importance in the estimates of this department that it totals over half a million dollars. But when we come to the first item, and seek, for this committee of the whole, information which any intelligent committee ought to have before it undertakes to approve a request for another 150,000 under the first item concerning publicity and information, the minister is not able to furnish the committee with the expenditure under this item last year. Here it is May 34, two montns after the close of the fiscal year, and we are told that it is not within the power of the minister to tell this committee what the expenditures under this item were during the fiscal year ended March 31, 1946. As a new member of this house, I say that that statement shocks me. We are asked to vote $50,000 on this item alone, and over half a million dollars on similar items scattered throughout the items for this department. On this first item alone it is not within the power of the minister to give the committee this information. It would not have surprised me if the minister had said, "I have not this information before me, but I shall have it for the committee on Monday." But the minister did not answer that he did not have the information; he answered that the information was not available.
If the committee of the whole is to have to do business in that way it might just as well fold up and decide to pass these items holus-bolus. A lot of general information, is not of the slightest value. We are sent here for a
Supply-Health and Welfare

purpose; we are sent here to review estimates that total between three and1 four billion dollars. Are we not to be expected to apply even elementary business sense to a task of that kind? We asked for information about the expenditure last year under this item and we were told it is not available. We are now two months beyond the close of the fiscal year.
That is not all. Last night I suggested that it would be of -assistance to the house in discharging its duties in connection with these estimates if the House set up a committee of reasonable size which could get information first hand from the officials of the department. Surely the officials of the department are not made of fragile glass. They do not need to be insulated from members of parliament. Surely to goodness, we have a sense of responsibility and we can bear that sense of responsibility in mind when we are in committee. Why should it be so necessary to insulate these officials of the department from the members of the house, especially when it comes to seeking information which I say should be before us if this committee is to do its duty in connection with these estimates?
Last night I put forward the idea that there ought to be a standing committee on health, welfare and social security, which could review the estimates of this department, not with a view to depriving this committee of supply of its proper opportunities to consider the estimates but rather to supplement its work, to assist it and to get information first hand from the officials of the department. Apparently that was not approved by the minister. What do we find to-night? When the hon. member for Vaneouver-Burrard asked for information about these items, what was he told? In connection with the publicity items totalling half a million dollars he was told that they were put in-I think I am quoting the words of the minister-by the officials of the depatrment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: That is not so at all.

That was the significance of the minister's remarks as conveyed to me, and I made an immediate note of them. Would it not be a good idea for the members, not in any spirit of hositility-I do not want anyone to get that impression at all-but with a view to discharging our duty, to get information and to apply our intelligence based on that information to a review of these estimates to see whether they are reasonable and should be passed and approved. How can we do that when we do not get information, when we are told that these items were put in by the officials of the department?

I should like very much to have an opportunity of asking the officials of the department about the method by which they arrived at these substantial figures. I should like to ask them, what are the programmes, the well thought-out and carefully integrated programmes which they ought to have had in mind, yes even as far advanced as the blueprint stage, long before they asked the minister to take the responsibility of going before the treasury board and asking for substantial amounts of money under the heading of information and publicity? Would that not be the responsible course? Would that not be a course that would permit this House of Commons to do its duty?
A word in conclusion about the general attitude toward this and other items in the minister's estimates. I tried to make it perfectly clear last night that we of the official opposition attach the utmost importance to the work of this department. I think I indicated that we had the view that there are no two more important aspects of government administration than health and welfare. Therefore, let no one say that it is in any spirit of hostility to health and welfare that we approach our duty with regard to these estimates. I indicated last night, and I repeat now, that in approaching these estimates we want information. We want to be sure that what is asked for here will represent the soundest application of the taxpayer's dollar, that the taxpayer is going to get value in good administration of health and good administration of welfare services for the dollar he is being asked to pay.
We are going to have the budget before us before very long, we hope. What are we to be told by the Minister of Finance when w-e come to discuss taxes? I think it is fair to say that if the minister recommends any reduction in taxation he will say that that can be done only to the extent that we are prepared to spend less. If he does not recommend any reduction in taxes he will probably say that he could not do so because the house has insisted on large expenditures for certain services that are considered by the house to be necessary. Would it not be helpful to the Minister of Finance; would it not be helpful to ourselves if we weighed in the light of common sense and in the light of information, which we do not seem to have at the present time, these expenditures that we are being asked to pass?
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, speaking of the duty and functions of this department to provide and disseminate educational information throughout Canada,

Supply-Health and Welfare
said that what we need is not less information, but more information. Those are true words, and if I might add to them I would say that what wre need is the best possible information. It is only when we get the best possible information that shall have the best application of the taxpayer's dollar. The minister has said, and rightly, that our health problem to-day is, in effect, to close the gap between what we know and what we do, that that is the way to meet the killers of humanity. I wonder how much this department is contributing to the elimination of those killers by this May "filler" issued by the department:
Better health and greater happiness for children are expected to result from wise spending of the family allowance it is stated by officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare, Ottawa. A family's basic needs include adequate food, clothing, shelter and medical supervision. Family allowance officials suggest that, when all these things have been provided, parents use what is left of their income on extras calculated to add zest to living.
Is it making the wisest application of the taxpayer's dollar, the dollar which the Minister of Finance may be trying to conserve when he brings in his budget, to tell the people of Canada to use the money paid out in family allowances to add zest to living? Is there a member of this house who thinks that is adding to the education or information of the people of Canada on necessary matters of health, to be told to use the remainder of the family allowances to add zest to living? I hope, Mr. Chairman, that is not a fair sample of the kind of publicity which is being issued by this department. I hope it is not a fair sample of the way in which the taxpayers are being called upon to contribute over half a million dollars to the publicity channels alone of this department.
I do not wish to prolong this discussion. I think the issue is perfectly clear. But I do want in all good part to say to the minister that we have important estimates of his department to review. We do not intend to approach them in any spirit of hostility, but we want to see the money spent wisely on health and welfare, and so far as we can be satisfied that the money is to be devoted to wise purposes we shall be back of his programme to a man. But we shall want a lot more information than we have yet been given.
I ask the minister now, with a week-end ahead of us, if before this committee proceeds to consider the detailed items of his estimates he will provide the house with information on all expenditures of his department for publicity last year; that is the fiscal 63260-132
year ended March 31, 1946, in all these branches in which we are asked to approve appropriations for publicity and information. In the second place, will he give the committee the expenditures made by this department during the fiscal year ended March 31, 1946, for publicity and information representing payments made outside of departmental salaries, that is to persons outside the department, and to whom these amounts were paid, and what the amounts were? I think the committee will receive that information with appreciation.
There has been enough said in all parts of the house, at least by those who sit on this side of the house, to make it clear to the minister that we want to see carried on a greatly extended programme of research. There is great hope in the realm of research, and if it comes to choosing between expenditures on research and expenditures on publicity of this kind I think it is the duty of the house to make it quite clear to the minister for his guidance and that of the government in future that we would rather see the money spent on research. Where money can be spent wisely on education, let it be spent, but spend it wisely.

Mr. Chairman, this is the first time that I have spoken on this department. I can assure you I have listened with a great deal of interest to those who have preceded me. It seems to me that the one great plea that has been made by all speakers is that the function of the Department of National Health and Welfare should be widened in its scope, that it should become more effective, that we should have more research, that other types of health service should be set up, and especially should we try to facilitate the cure of those who are suffering from such maladies as arthritis, cancer and other diseases which are looked upon as being more or less incurable.
I rise to mention what may appear to be a rather tiny thing but one which some speakers have overlooked. I refer particularly to the security of those sufferers, perhaps incurable, who because of their financial circumstances are thrown upon either charitable institutions or perhaps upon their civic governments to receive assistance in the form of relief, which, after all, is a pittance, or else have to rely upon the good graces of friends or perhaps their relatives who are not in a position to keep them. I think we could all cite a good many such cases. The minister may feel that this does not primarily come within his department, but his department is known as the Department of National

Supply-Health and Welfare

Health and Welfare and the minister is due sooner or later to put through a measure of social security.
I had several cases brought to me last year, one that I am particularly well acquainted with. This young woman was afflicted with infantile paralysis, and it was found, after some considerable treatment through the programme of the Alberta government, that nothing much could be done for her because the disease had gone too far. She is one of ' the finest types of young women I have ever met. Her mother is a widow. This young woman wrote to me and said, "Mr. Hansell, what am I going to do? Is my widowed mother to keep me for the rest of my life?" That is only one case, but I am certain that it could be duplicated thousands and thousands of times in Canada.
I had another case of an epileptic woman. Her mother and father were on the old age pension. She said, "My only help is from my mother and father." I speak for these people because, while these cases may not be so numerous as others, and they are scattered throughout the length and breadth of this land, they have no organization. It is almost impossible for these incurables to bring into existence an organization that can present their case and mobilize public opinion behind them. Yet I suppose there is not a member of parliament sitting here to-night, or sitting anywhere else on this Friday night, who is not just as anxious about these cases as I am. I think we are all agreed that something should be done for them, and I plead on their behalf that something should be done for them. I know I have the support of parliament. I would ask the minister what he is prepared to do for them. Are they still to be considered as indigents, a word that has fallen into miserable disrepute? Are they to be considered as relief recipients, another term that has fallen into disrepute? Surely our country and civilization are worth more than that. I ask the minister what he or his government is prepared to do for these unfortunate people; I do not know what his answer is going to be.
Nearly everyone who has spoken to-day has raised his voice on behalf of patients afflicted with cancer, arthritis and rheumatic diseases. I am not going to repeat their pleas; I would just, add mine as one more voice, one more pleading voice, perhaps a "still small voice" that is "crying in the wilderness", but surely 245 voices all crying in the same wilderness should bring forth some results.
rMr. Hansell.]
I was particularly interested in the speech this afternoon .of the hon. member for Lethbridge. I really think he put the minister on the spot. As he was speaking I fancied he was a mind-reader and could almost tell beforehand what the minister's reply would be. When the -minister rose to reply to these pleading voices, I thought he was floundering around, probably because the hon. member for Lethbridge had stolen some of his thunder. When the minister had finished his reply I wondered whether I dared send out Hansard to these people who had written in asking us to lift our voices on their behalf. I could imagine the young woman whom I have referred to as an infantile paralysis case, the paralytic girl I have in mind, and a host of others getting copies of Hansard, looking at the index to find the Department of National Health and Welfare, turning over the pages anxiously to see what the government was going to do for them, and then reading the minister's speech.
And your remarks, too.

Yes, and my remarks too. What a disappointment they would have! I believe they would put Hansard aside and say, "Well, I suppose we shall have to await another election for a few more promises, and perhaps by the time I am an old woman"- or, an old man-"I may get an extra few dollars." It seems to me that that is all the minister's answer amounted to.
I appreciated what the hon. member for Lethbridge said as to what was the source of the minister's trouble, and I am confident that he was right. All of us want our people to be healthy; all of us want clinics to be established and research to be proceeded with. But it costs money. That is where the "sticker" is, and let us admit it; the minister does not know where to get the wherewithal to finance these projects. He said that the solution offered by this Social Credit group is a solution of "funny money." I believe Hansard will record that he made that statement- "funny money"-and of course he was not going to use that and put the economy of Canada into, I think he said, a "jackpot" or something like that.
Let me ask him one or two questions. How does he know that the money we would propose to get is funny money? And how does he know that if he used a few million dollars of national money, issued without debt to the taxpayer and the country, he would upset our

Supply-Health and Welfare
whole economy or put it into a jackpot or a cocked hat or whatever term he wants to use? How does he know?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Ask yourself the same question.

My suggestion is this, try it and see. I am not saying that he should go to the Bank of Canada and say, "Mr. Banker, give us a billion dollars"; I am asking him to go there for a few paltry millions. We have been talking throughout the war years in terms of billions. Let him go and ask for $5,000,000.
Let him make it a little more than that.
Why, $5,000,000 is just chicken feed.
Some chicken.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Social Credit feed.

I expect my congregations in the churches where I preach to come forward with a little more than chicken feed. Let him try this; let him ask for $10,000,000. Surely that is only a drop in the bucket.
Do I understand that the Minister of Finance poked his head in the curtain and then pulled it back again?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: My hon. friend is just saying that to bolster up his speech.
That actually happened.
Yes, that actually happened.

I did not hear the Minister of Labour. When I was a boy we used to go out snaring gophers. We put the snare around the top of the hole; there we would stay for one minute, two minutes, five minutes, maybe fifteen minutes, and when that gopher put his head up through the hole we would pull, very often only to find that the gopher was a little faster than we were. I think that was the case with the Minister of Finance; perhaps he pulled his head in before I could pull the snare.
Let the government ask the Bank of Canada to bring in a little legislation which will issue, free of debt, about $10,000,000-surely that is not going to upset the whole economy of the country-and see what effect it has. I challenge them to do that and prove whether or not that money would be phoney money and whether the issuance of it would knock the economy of this country into a cocked hat. I challenge the minister to do that. Just a paltry $10,000,000, chicken feed.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Why not make it $10 billion? If you want to be foolish, be foolish.
63260-132J	4 Q5

You would be afraid to do that. I would not want the minister to do it with a palpitating heart, fearing he is going to ruin the economy of the country. I am suggesting $10,000,000, mere chicken feed. I am suggesting that he pay it out for national health. That is not very much to spend for such a purpose. If he does not do it, this country should know that he regards the mighty and holy dollar as more sacred than the health and welfare of our children.
I think that is a good place to stop.

Just one brief word before we pass this item. Since my speech on cancer this afternoon I have been making a brief examination of the annual report of the department of public health of Alberta, and from what I see there I have every reason to congratulate that province on the splendid progress it has made in developing cancer clinics. It was not my intention this afternoon to make any invidious comparisons between provinces, but I would say this. If there is to be a race between one province and another to see which develops the best cancer clinics, I am all for it. Saskatchewan has set up free clinics, free in very sense of the word, free diagnosis, free X-rays, free radium treatment and free surgical treatment, without any limits, for rich and poor alike.
Free hospitalization?
Yes, and free hospitalization, without limit and absolutely without cost. It is my hope that every province will do likewise in order to defeat this terrible scourge.

There is one thing I would ask the minister to do. It does not come within his department and the budget is no doubt being prepared. When it is brought down I hope the minister will use his influence with the Department of Finance to see if we cannot get invalid equipment brought into the country duty free. I know that certain types of chairs, bed-tables and so on, used by invalids, come under a fairly high rate of duty, and I think this is one place where it would cost the government very little and would bring a good deal of relief to people who have sickness in their families. I mean the placing on the free list of equipment of that type for the assistance of invalids. I will support any appropriation that is made to assist in the study of cancer, rheumatic diseases, sclerosis and those mysterious diseases which afflict so many people at the present time, but I would ask the minister if this might be kept in mind when the budget is brought down.

Surely the minister will reply to the request for information from the
Supply-Health and Welfare

hon. member for Eglinton. He has requested certain information which in the past in other departments has undoubtedly been forthcoming-the amount expended under the vote in 'the previous fiscal year. Surely the minister will comply with that request.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
In reply to the member for Rosetown-Biggar, as he probably knows, the Department of Veterans Affairs has succeeded in securing the entry of such equipment for veterans, and I have been greatly interested lately in receiving representations by the veterans themselves that they would be glad to see such equipment imported free into Canada for other than ex-soldiers. I shall be glad indeed to see every possible consideration given the representation. -
With regard to the questions of the hon. member for Eglinton, I have not, I hope, given the impression that I was not willing to give any information, or that I was finding it difficulty to give any. It is perfactly possible, given time, to secure information on any expenditure by the government; and when I gave the figure before, of the expenditure made under this vote of $2,421, that was the figure I had before me. Since then, however, I have sent out for further information, and I find that we have a figure for the period up to March 31, 1946 of a total expenditure for the year of $24,959.68. Also, I afn told that the unexpended balance at March 31, 1946, of $25,040.32 was committed for in part, although the accounts were not submitted and therefore not paid, and since the vote expired the amount due on the commitment will have to be paid out of the 1946-47 publicity vote. In this connection there is, as I explained, I hope to the satisfaction of the committee, quite a wide demand for a wide variety of publicity activities, which it is not possible to allocate under the different departmental heads such as nutrition, tuberculosis, venereal disease, child and maternal hygiene and the like, and it is necessary to provide for their general alloca-lion. This vote is used for that purpose. I shall be glad indeed to obtain from the treasury, as the figures become available, anything that my hon. friend wants. As he knows, every member is entitled to that and he will get it. It is just a question of availability at any particular moment. He must realize that it is not possible for one to carry with him into the house the breakdown of every expenditure up to date. I hope, therefore, that with that explanation it will be agreed that the item should pass; and in view of the interest he has taken, and which other hon. members have shown in these items, I shall endeavour to obtain the information

from the officers of the department and the treasury and have them available when these estimates next come before the house.
Just one further word. The hon. member seemed to suggest that the officers of the department were responsible for the estimates. He must know that the deputy ministers draw up the estimates after consultation with their officials, as a result of vreeks and months of work, having regard to what they plan, what they sp,end and what they expect to do, and in the light of the over-all position. It is then taken up with the minister and, when signed by him, is put before the treasury and then ultimately brought before parliament. I hope the hon. member did not suggest that there was anything wrong with officials putting forward estimates. There is no other way in which it can be done at the initial stage, but the estimates must, of course, be put forward by the deputy ministers, and by the ministers before parliament.
One word in reply to the hon. member for Macleod. I would be very glad indeed if I could give him all the assurances he wants, both on fiscal and other matters, but in regard to disability benefits we did have a debate in the house, and I indicated what I considered would be the right view at that particular moment, on that occasion. I do not think he would want me to go over it at this time; but I must say that I have, as everyone has, the utmost sympathy for the people who are afflicted as those are whom he had in mind. It is a question of what agency should look after them. If it is decided that it should be some agency other than that which it always has been, then I think it is something for the provinces and the dominion to agree to. Until that is done all we can do is to continue to administer the laws in accordance wnth the constitution.

I am glad that my hon. friends to the right insisted on an explanation of the vote that was brought up by the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard. When the minister gave the explanation that of the $50,000 vote he could account for $2,400 which had been expended up to December 31, 1945, I thought it was the most amazing answer that I had ever heard given this house over a period of fifteen years. So far as hon. members are concerned, these estimates are important or they are not. A mere item in the estimates does not mean anything to a member unless he has an explanation of what it is for. Indeed, a member should not pass such an item unless he knows what use is to be made of it.
I am not at all satisfied with the explanation given by the minister a moment ago as to how

Supply-health and Welfare
these estimates are arrived at. Surely he does not arrive at an estimate by saying or have someone from his staff say that we shall put down $50,000 for this and $25,000 for that and so on. Surely, when an estimate of $50,000 or of any amount is put down under any particular head there is before the minister a description, not a complete itemized account as to how it is to be spent, but at least an indication of what is to be done with it. It seems to me that is the only way that an item makes any sense when it comes here, and the only way in which the minister can make it real to the members of the committee. That is why I suggested, since this is a new department, that a break-down of the item of last year, which I insist the minister ought to have before him when he came into the committee, would be the easiest way to arrive at whether or not the money was well spent.
I do not want to draw any invidious comparisons between one minister and another. Certainly I do not wish to do that so far as the present minister is concerned. I did not take any part in the discussion of the estimates of the department which were before the committee for about a week. I am sure that those who did take part in that discussion found that they got about all the information they could be given, and I do not see any reason why we should not receive the same information from the department with which we are now dealing.
I wish to say a few words on the general subject which has been discussed to-night. I find it difficult to understand my Social Credit friends. If my memory serves me aright, I believe that one of them said in a public speech a few days ago that that country was governed best that wras governed least. If that is a good maxim to go by, surely we should not ask in the next breath that the minister of health or any minister should inject himself and his department into every phase of our economic, cultural and social life. Either we want a government to do things or we do not. I take the position which was taken a little earlier in the evening, perhaps in a different way, that the government is an agency of the people which does for the people collectively what they are not able to do for themselves individually. The moment our affairs reach the stage in any department where the collective will and the collective effort of the people can be mobilized to do the thing which individually we are no longer able to do for ourselves, then at that moment that thing is ripe for government action. Our health affairs have in many respects, perhaps not all, reached that stage. I do not believe-if I ever did, it was a wrong
belief-that health is a matter that can be maintained by doctors. I believe the more doctors you have, the more disease.
Some lion. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.
The diseases of your grandparents and their parents were few and simple.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We had no doctors.

We had no doctors. When you multiply your doctors you multiply the number of diseases, and if you are not sick before you see a doctor you will be sick afterwards. That will continue to be the state of affairs until, as some hon. member said this afternoon, the doctor becomes an educator who will tell the people how to maintain health rather than try to cure people when through their bad habits they get into ill health.
There is not an hon. member in this chamber to-night who does not know that by his own actions he can make himself sick within the next day or so. He knows equally well-
Oh, oh.

Every intelligent person knows that if he takes care he can preserve his' health and feel fit from day to day. I believe in public health. I believe that fresh air and the plentiful use of soap and water da more to promote health than anything else.
Just water?

I always insist on drinking water. That is why I keep my health. You cannot take it out of a bottle with a spoon or from a pill in a bottle or a box you carry in your pocket. If we and the minister are to deal with this matter effectively we shall have to work to get the cooperation of the provinces so that we can have a national health system. I thought under the then Minister of Pensions and National Health, with the efforts that were made in 1942 and, I think, in 1943-the fact that we were coming to an election in those days may have had nothing to do with it-we were really moving toward a national health system for Canada. I do not knowT why the thing has fallen down, why it is to be thrown away now after so much very good work has been done. The staff of the former department did excellent work, and we should carry on with that work, despite certain set-backs, until we convince the people of Canada that a national health system will pay for itself.

I almost got shut out to-night by being a gentleman, and I am going to quit acting that way. I want to
Supply-Health and Welfare

say a few things under the general item which cannot be said under the item concerning child and maternal welfare, on which I intend to speak again. I wish to congratulate the minister on bringing to this country from England a distinguished person, Sir Wilson Jameson. It was a very great privilege to listen to him, and I only regret that all hon. members of this house did not attend the meeting in the railway committee room.
We were practically all there.
If you were I did not see you.
I was amazed myself.

I thought it was a great advantage to have first-hand the plans of the government of Great Britain and the marvellous example they are setting the world. Here we have this devastated country, which had one-third of its homes damaged or destroyed, undertaking a great rehousing programme with public money.
We are giving them the money.

I am coming to that. They are undertaking subsidized housing, so that even the poorest people can live in decent houses even if they cannot pay economic rents. These people who are undertaking this terrific thing in housing are now undertaking a terrific thing in public health. I think this is the valuable thing the British people do. They meet a need and establish a precedent; that is the British tradition which I am proud to own. Here we have the British people, in the hour of their extremity, amid the ruins of their homes and their country, planning to supply forty million people with complete coverage, while we in this country, who did not have one home destroyed; who have more equipment and a greater production potential and greater wealth than we had before the war are still denying help to the poor arthritics, the victims of infantile paralysis, the victims of cancer, the victims of any one of a hundred other things which can kill y&u-and you will be just as dead. Here we are still saying we do not know where we are to get the money. I think we need education, but even more I believe we need some political education in this country, the sort of thing that will tell the people that Great Britain now has undertaken to own, in the name of all the people, the basic industries and to spend for the good of all the people the revenue
fMrs. Strum.]
derived from their operation. I have in my hand a clipping from the Ottawa Citizen containing a news dispatch dated May 14, 1946, from the London representative of that newspaper, outlining the objectives and the accomplishments of the Labour government of Great Britain. It says:
1.	Every man, woman and child will get free medical attention under a national health scheme and every general practitioner will be working for the state at an average salary of $4,500.
2,	Apart from this national health scheme, the social security of every Briton, regardless of financial status, will be guaranteed by the state from the day of his birth to the day of his death and including allowances to mothers before- the babies are born.
It goes on to say that England will now have state-owned and state-operated coal mines, and goes through the whole catalogue of resources of England from which the people will now enjoy the revenue. They will own the great public utilities of England; the revenue will go into the treasury and will be returned to the people in housing, in health and in well-being. That is the sort of education I am interested in. That is the sort of education I intend to carry on inside and outside this house as long as I am able to do so, because the people of this country need to be told that this government refuses to undertake the technique that will replenish the treasury so that adequate funds may be given to the Minister of Health and Welfare, who is now doing an execellent job, with the limited resources his party allows him to have, in looking after the health of this country.
I believe in public education. We have all kinds of voluntary organizations doing excellent work. For twenty years I belonged to the women's institutes of my province. For twenty years we circulated petitions and passed resolutions, until we were black in the face. We asked for better old age pensions, for mothers' allowances, for blood testing of both contracting parties before marriage, for free textbooks, for free cancer care. These simple, sensible human needs of the people we asked for again and again; we carried on public education, but it was not until our province got political education and elected a C.C.F. government that we got all these things. And we got them in one year. To-day our financial position is better than it has ever been in the history of the province, regardless of the fact that we had a severe drought last year. You need only consult the bond markets to see that our bonds have hit a new high. We have retired a sizeable chunk of the public debt, and our sinking fund is much greater than it was two years ago.

Questions
It is true that education is a necessary thing, but I did not notice any campaign of education about this time last year directed toward family allowances. I did not know of any widespread demand for them, unless it was from the party I represent, because ever since I was in New Zealand five years ago I have been talking about family allowances. We got family allowances, but I submit that the Prime Minister did a good thing for a bad reason. That was' not preceded by years of public education, either. So I submit that political education is the thing this country lacks most of all.
Item stands.
Progress reported.
